articles.title: 🤷‍♀️ Soul Searching Amid Tech Frustrations
articles.description: Alright it’s time to check in. I have wanted to share some findings between now and my last post, but...
articles.body_html:
Alright it’s time to check in. I have wanted to share some findings between now and my last post, but I have been too preoccupied playing catching up with school work and zip-tying my online shop together. I say zip-tie, because that is what it feels like at this point. I am feeling a little burnt at the moment, so I am going to protest by sharing my drama.

There is a couple things I want to talk about:

  • everfluorescent.com
  • Optimizing Google tools for small business
  • Creative atrophy
  • Judgement, fear, and failure

everfluorescent.com

Last you heard from me, I had taken on quite an undertaking of configuring my home network with a Juniper switch. It has been smooth sailing so far. (My development server has turned into a tiny production server and it must be saved at all costs.) 😂 Protect the tiny server! I have actually impressed myself that my switch is buzzing along, doing its thing.

An unexpected feeling has reared its head from this experience. I realize that I now sit cozily tucked behind multiple firewalls. Paired with multiple sources of traffic monitoring, I think this is boss mode. Look at me protecting and analyzing. I did not plan for this. 😂 I just wanted to play with CSS all day but here we are. 🤷‍♀️ Remember: do not get too cozy!

Upon getting my network recombobulated, I went straight back to my website checklist. On that list was creating unified location for managing social media posts. As you know, there are too many and it is a lot to deal with. That is why big companies hire social media managers and content creators. However, I do not really consider myself a content creator. When I think of content creators, (and please forgive me here if this is your profession) some images come to mind:

  • Well endowed females selling a ‘lose weight fast’ or ‘skin care’ product comes to mind. It’s not realistic and we know it.
  • Soccer mom gets organized with new travel mug that has pockets for essentials in its carrying case and all of her children wear clothing that have tracking devices sewn into the seams because she is karen 2.0.

I think you get the idea. 😂😂

Basically, the idea of ‘content creation’ causes me to do an internal eye roll. Dude, I am an artist, I am already a creator. But now there has to be two of me? I really groan at the idea of additionally having to market myself. I came to realize that I actually have a ton of raw content - pictures, videos, stories - they just need to be re-organized and published in a way that makes sense to the public.

Feeling overwhelmed, I started to look for free tools or tools with free tiers that could help me manage this situation. Without too much explaining, here is what I’ve landed on so far:

Custom Stack

  • Buffer: Add up to 3 social media sites for free for scheduled content posting to rebuild brand awareness. I added Facebook, Instagram and TikTok to Buffer’s free tier.
  • Custom spreadsheet with several columns of data including date to be published, platform, links for media, text, status, and others.
  • A Google bot service that reads from my spreadsheet when called (manually, from terminal) The bot schedules the posts for me in Buffer, changes the status for each row when appropriate, which lets me know if it has been added to the cue or not. The Google bot cannot use a Google drive link to upload media links to Buffer. However, it can read them and put them somewhere else. The Google bot takes the media from my chosen Google drive folder, uploads the media to a Cloudflare R2 storage container, then loads them into Buffer from Cloudflare. Media files in Cloudflare are automatically deleted after 30 days, keeping it clean.
  • Canva: great for making short videos with content I already have. I do not need to be the next Steven King, I just need to have some effective communication here, on a very small time budget. This fits the bill. Thank you, templates.
  • Brevo: Promotional email management

Google Analytics Tall Tale

Now I am not some big fancy super analytics boss, but I do have tools. We can build amazing things with the right tools. Let me tell you my Google Analytics tall tale.

In a previous post, I shared the 404/redirect nightmare I was having. Years of trying to do online business left me with a ton of redirects and broken links. Broken links were found in an old shopify account that was connected to social medias, other places I rarely had used like X, pinterest, square, and other deeply nested what-have-yous. Customers were being sent to an empty room. I found that out, the hard way. Since then, I have cleaned up my act and spent a lot of time refining things where appropriate.

That involved:

  • Shutting down my shopify fully
  • Removing or updating links in various platforms

I have been trying to understand why I was getting so much traffic but almost no sales. This fix was only part of the problem, I learned later. Continuing on through time, I checked my Google analytics and ads daily. My money was still being spent, with no improvement in sales. However I did feel better that the 404s have almost ceased to exist. 😂🤷‍♀️ But this obviously needs further intervention. So what is the deal, Google? I had to allow some time to pass to get actual data now that the redirect and 404 nightmare was cleaned up. I let a week or so pass, then I summoned Claude to check Supermetrics while my free tier was still working. I learned ALOT.

Sure, pay for Google ads they say, increase your reach, blah blah blah. It is so much more than that. You can not just pay $5, $10, or $100 and get a sale. You must analyze clicks and traffic to optimize your money and ultimately, supposedly, your business’s success.

This is a new area for me. I am flying by the seat of my chair and clinging on for dear life, wondering how much of my own pocket will deplete before the beast becomes sustainable.

There is no promise, no guarantee, just a million miles of the internet. How do we clear the digital weeds?

Digital Weeds

As it turns out, SEO is not enough. You think you mastered that? Good job. Time for phase two: target practice. Upon drawing data for something like the 20th time in my free trial, Claude reported back to me that the majority of my money was being wasted on garbage clicks. Excuse me, Google? What are you doing, bro? Ahem Garbage clicks, sir? 🤣🤣🤣 You are going to just waste money like that? We all want to blame everyone but ourselves, it is human nature. When I learned that money was quite literally being wasted, and having the prior knowledge of customers being sent to 404’s, a thought occurred to me: “For the past few months, I have been paying for customers that are not interested, to go no where.”

People were clicking my ads after searching for things like “cat carrying hoodie” and other oddities.

This is where I learned the importance of negative keywords in Google searches. Searches that are not related to your product generally should not result in your product ad appearing. That is admittedly bad marketing. You can add negative keywords to help refine when your ads appear after a Google search, to help you reach the right audience.

I checked my Google ads spending before and after refining keywords with Supermetrics. Clicks are down but spending is still up, so I’m turning off AI Max since it is likely resulting in my brand appearing for other brand searches, cool, but expensive. I’m also turning off ‘Search Partners’ as well as that could be a source of unrelated expensive clicks. I have also crimped my budget extremely for the time being until I get a grasp on traffic and clicks.

Some may view this as a failure and waste of money, but what actually happened was a tremendous amount of learning the landscape. Throwing myself into a fire and learning is tremendously more beneficial than saving a bit of cash in the here and now. I bit that bullet for you, so any new aspiring web developer with a plan does not have to. If you already know your broad search terms and negative keywords ahead of time, then you are a step ahead. Retrospectively, I would try to gather all the data you can on your intended audience and have a chat with your favorite AI agent before deciding to spend money on ads. Just do not be surprised when it requires continued refinement! And please if you are not experienced use the Supermetrics free trial with your agent. It does a lot of heavy lifting! Do not make it more difficult than it has to be.

The Fun Updates

It is not all analytical doom and gloom, I had my significant other craft me a shiny new version of my logo for the hero area on my website. And I must say, it is freaking awesome.

I have also added some more images of my art in the gallery area for viewing. That is found at https://www.everfluorescent.com/gallery and consists of only my bigger fancier pieces at the moment.

I have also added some policy pages to comply with Google merchant centers requirements, which are now found at the bottom of the page. In addition, I have included a proper signup area for promotions. If you signup and verify your email, you get a unique code for $5 off. I have been wanting this feature added for some time now, and I have found that managing it through Brevo on the free tier for now works just fine. It was not hard to set up and I highly recommend giving that a whirl if you are in need of managing promotional email.

In addition, A tiny blog area in the about section has been added. Two existing stories from my old square site were refined and placed there. This is an area that I will be working on through time.

Social media links have been updated on the page, and set the repo to private. Sorry guys, I would love to keep sharing, but I am sure you understand.

Customer Confidence Concerns

  • Data is stored in another location.
  • Financials are all handled through Stripe, a reputable transaction handling partner.
  • Google Places API to pulls in actual Google reviews, I’ve been doing this a while! Social media efforts will slowly bring brand awareness and direct customers to my site.

Unrelated Contemplations

Last night, I got absorbed into a new painting, nothing big or fancy, just wanted to get out of my head. I have been doing the “tech world” thing for nearly 4 years. I completed an apprenticeship, went back to school for second bachelors, and worked multiple IT jobs. Here I sit now again, unemployed, in front of a canvas and computer screen.

Years ago, I used to dye my hair brilliant colors, neon, galaxy, whatever striking color I was obsessed with at the time. Knowing about the conservative nature of corporate environments and harsh barriers to entry for a junior dev, I dyed my hair a “natural” color with a conservative hair style and maintained that image the last 4 years while I tried to be a “professional”. If I can say one real fact, it is that I had more money when I was out there being myself, with lime green rainbow hair.

I have refrained from doing certain things for years in case an opportunity arose. But considering the lack of opportunity despite my best efforts, I am about to not care again. I have also navigated a lot of other things during this time. I went into hiding, dark mode, quiet. I feel that “trying to be perfect so much as to never even get a speeding ticket” has gotten me no where. I stopped posting on social media so that certain people would stop digitally attacking me, to say the least. It has been years, and I am tired of it. Tired of being a ghost, tired of hiding, tired of being perfect, and not dying my hair fun colors for what? The interviews and job offers that do not exist? 🤣 This is insanity, and I want to express myself how I deem warranted. If you judge me based on my neon hair - I am not sorry I blinded you. Get some sunglasses. However, natural hair color is low maintenance, and was an optimal choice for turbulent times.

What do you think - should I be myself - or continue to seek and wait for opportunity? Tell me, what are the current thoughts of society for professional visual aesthetic?

articles.title: 9 Transactional Email Mistakes That Show Up in Production
articles.description: Nine transactional email mistakes that cause missing receipts, duplicate sends, and expired password resets, with practical fixes for retries, DNS, suppressions, and webhooks.
articles.body_html:
Your checkout succeeds, but the receipt never arrives. A customer clicks “resend” and gets two copies. A password reset lands twenty minutes later, after the link has expired.

A successful test email tells you little about how the integration behaves under failure. Production adds timeouts, retries, process crashes, DNS changes, and delivery events that arrive after your application has moved on.

Here are nine mistakes worth checking before your users discover them. The examples use SMTPfast, but the application patterns apply across email providers.

1. Treating an API success response as proof of delivery

This is an easy shortcut to ship:

await emailProvider.send(message);
await markReceiptDelivered(order.id);

The provider accepted your request. Your application immediately records that the customer received the receipt.

Those are different events.

Submission, recipient-server acceptance, inbox placement, and reading are separate stages. Even a successful SMTP handoff does not establish that a message appeared in someone’s inbox. SMTP defines responsibility for accepting and transporting a message; it does not provide a read receipt. RFC 5321

The fix: record what you actually know.

Start with an application delivery record containing:

notification_id
business_event_id
provider_email_id
submitted_at
delivered_at
bounced_at
last_error

Store the provider’s email ID when submission succeeds. Update delivery information from webhooks or reconciliation jobs.

For example, SMTPfast exposes message details and delivery events through GET /v1/emails/:id. That gives support a path from an order to the provider’s recorded outcome. Emails API

A useful support answer is: “The recipient server accepted it at 14:32.” “Our API call succeeded” leaves most of the investigation unfinished.

2. Sending email inside the HTTP request

A checkout handler often starts like this:

const order = await saveOrder(input);
await sendReceipt(order);
return response.json(order);

Now provider latency affects checkout latency.

If sending fails after the order commits, the customer may see an error even though the purchase succeeded. If the process crashes between saving the order and sending the receipt, the order exists without any durable record that email remains to be sent.

Moving the send into an untracked background promise leaves the crash problem intact.

The fix: write the business change and an outbox record in the same database transaction.

This simplified SQL illustrates the boundary:

BEGIN;

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total_cents)
VALUES (:order_id, :customer_id, :total_cents);

INSERT INTO email_outbox (
    notification_id,
    business_event_id,
    kind,
    status
)
VALUES (
    :notification_id,
    :order_id,
    'order_receipt',
    'pending'
);

COMMIT;

A worker claims pending rows and submits the emails.

Use a uniqueness constraint for the logical notification, such as (business_event_id, kind, recipient_id), so processing the same business event twice does not create two receipts.

The worker also needs a recoverable claim or lease. If it dies mid-send, another worker must eventually be able to continue.

That recovery introduces the next problem.

3. Retrying a timed-out send without an idempotency key

Consider this sequence:

Worker submits receipt
Provider accepts receipt
Response is lost
Worker records a timeout
Worker retries
Customer receives two receipts

A timeout means your application does not know the outcome. It does not prove that the provider rejected the message.

The fix: assign an idempotency key to the logical send and preserve it across attempts.

For a provider endpoint that supports it, the request might include:

Idempotency-Key: receipt:order_4821:v1

Generate and store the key before the first attempt. Reuse the same request body when retrying that operation.

This defeats the purpose:

// Every retry becomes a new operation.
const idempotencyKey = crypto.randomUUID();

SMTPfast documents a 24-hour idempotency window for its batch endpoint, with a conflict response if the same key is reused with a different body. Check the exact endpoint’s contract before relying on it. Batch sending documentation

Your database uniqueness constraint prevents duplicate jobs. Provider idempotency addresses repeated submission after an uncertain outcome. You need both boundaries.

Once the provider’s deduplication window expires, an unresolved send needs reconciliation or an explicit decision about duplicate risk.

4. Retrying until a useful email becomes a useless one

A receipt delayed by ten minutes can still help.

A password reset delivered after its token expires sends the user straight back to support.

Treating every notification as “retry until successful” ignores the lifetime of the action inside the message.

The fix: give each job a deadline and check its business state before submitting it.

For example:

kind: password_reset
created_at: 12:00
token_expires_at: 12:15
send_before: 12:10

The five-minute margin is an application choice, not a delivery guarantee. It leaves some time for downstream delivery and the user to act.

Before submission, check whether the job expired, the token was revoked, or a newer request superseded it.

Classify failures too:

Failure Worker action
Invalid payload Stop retrying; fix the request
Invalid credentials Alert; stop repeated attempts
Rate limit Reschedule using provider guidance
Temporary provider failure Retry with backoff and jitter
Timeout with unknown outcome Retry using the same idempotency key
Expired or superseded notification Mark expired or cancelled

SMTPfast supplies Retry-After on rate-limit responses. Respect it rather than letting every worker retry immediately. Rate limits documentation

An application deadline stops future submissions. It cannot recall a message already handed to the mail system.

5. Treating DNS authentication as a launch-day task

You verify the domain, send a test email, and close the ticket.

Months later, someone migrates DNS or removes an unfamiliar record. Authentication starts failing while the application continues submitting messages successfully.

The fix: make email DNS part of your infrastructure inventory and change review.

Keep these roles clear:

  • SPF authorizes sending infrastructure for the envelope sender domain.
  • DKIM signs messages using a signing domain.
  • DMARC checks whether passing SPF or DKIM aligns with the visible From domain and publishes a handling policy.

A passing SPF check for an unrelated domain does not, by itself, establish DMARC alignment. Google’s sender guidelines describe the alignment requirement for direct bulk email. Gmail sender guidelines

After a DNS migration, check the actual records and inspect authentication results on a received message.

Useful checks include:

dig +short TXT bounce.your-domain.com
dig +short TXT _dmarc.your-domain.com
dig +short CNAME your-selector._domainkey.your-domain.com

Replace those names with the hostnames your provider supplies.

Do not add a second SPF record at a hostname that already has one. Update the existing policy carefully. SMTPfast’s domain documentation covers this and the separate records used for its bounce subdomain. Domains documentation

6. Logging bounces and complaints without acting on them

A webhook arrives:

{
  "type": "email.bounced",
  "data": {
    "id": "email_abc123"
  }
}

Your handler writes a log line and returns success.

Tomorrow, the application tries the same address again.

The fix: make delivery feedback change application behavior.

A permanent bounce can mark an address as undeliverable and prompt the customer to correct it through another channel. A complaint should prevent continued sending according to your provider’s suppression policy.

Temporary delivery problems need different handling. Avoid treating every delayed message as a permanently invalid address.

SMTPfast automatically adds hard bounces and complaints to its suppression list and checks that list before sending. Your application should also use the outcome to stop creating futile jobs and explain the problem to users. Suppressions documentation

Do not automatically remove a suppression because a customer clicked “resend.” That button supplies no evidence that the underlying problem changed.

7. Applying the same unsubscribe rules to every email

A customer unsubscribes from a newsletter. Your application flips:

email_enabled = false

Later, they request a password reset. Your worker sees the flag and discards it.

One boolean has combined several unrelated decisions.

The fix: model marketing preferences separately from delivery eligibility.

For example:

marketing_opted_out
address_undeliverable
provider_suppressed

Then classify each notification by its actual purpose.

A newsletter opt-out should stop newsletters. A hard bounce still makes the address unusable for a receipt. Calling a promotion “transactional” does not make it an account notification.

With SMTPfast, unlabelled sends default to marketing. Explicitly set the category for genuine transactional messages:

{
  "category": "transactional"
}

Marketing-only suppressions allow those messages through; hard-bounce and complaint suppressions block both categories. Email categories, suppression scopes

Test this distinction directly: unsubscribe a test contact from marketing, then verify that an eligible transactional notification still follows the intended path.

8. Assuming webhook delivery happens exactly once

Your webhook handler updates the database, but the response never reaches the provider.

The provider retries. Your handler applies the same side effect again.

There is another failure window: the handler returns success, then crashes before saving the event. The provider considers delivery complete, but your application lost it.

The fix: authenticate the request, persist it durably, and make processing safe to repeat.

A useful sequence is:

Receive raw request
→ Verify signature
→ Persist event with a deduplication key
→ Return success
→ Process asynchronously

For SMTPfast, signature verification uses an HMAC over the raw request body. Parsing JSON and serializing it again can change the bytes being verified. Webhook verification documentation

Use a stable event identifier when the provider supplies one. Keep delivery-attempt identifiers separate. If the payload lacks an event ID, derive a deduplication strategy from the provider’s documented retry behavior.

Also avoid replacing the entire message state with whichever event arrived last. A delayed event should not erase a later delivery outcome.

SMTPfast retries unsuccessful webhook deliveries, so repeated requests are an expected integration path. Webhook retry documentation

9. Testing the template while skipping the failure paths

The preview looks good. The button works. The test message reaches your inbox.

That covers rendering and one successful send.

The worker, retry policy, and webhook handler need their own tests.

The fix: exercise the boundaries where work can be lost or repeated.

Test Expected behavior
Worker crashes before submission Job becomes eligible for processing again
Provider accepts; response is lost Retry preserves the idempotency key and body
Provider returns 429 Worker reschedules according to retry guidance
Same webhook arrives twice Side effects happen once
Database is unavailable during webhook receipt Handler does not acknowledge an unpersisted event
Reset job passes its deadline Worker marks it expired
Recipient has a hard-bounce suppression Worker does not keep resubmitting
Older event arrives late It does not overwrite newer delivery information

Use a fake provider for deterministic failure tests. Reserve real test sends for integration checks with addresses you control.

Give support a practical lookup path too: business event → notification → provider email ID → delivery history. Record the template version and timestamps, while keeping reset tokens and full message bodies out of routine logs.

For password resets and sign-in links, review click tracking as well. SMTPfast documents that tracked links pass through a redirect and their URLs are recorded; disable click tracking for links containing secrets. Tracking documentation

The next time you test transactional email, let one request time out after acceptance. Deliver a webhook twice. Stop the worker between submission and saving the response.

Those tests tell you whether the integration can survive the failures your users will eventually encounter.

articles.title: TypeScript `const` Enums Are Deprecated: What to Migrate to and Why the Compiler Team Made the Call
articles.description: The TypeScript compiler team deprecated const enums because they break isolated module compilation and cause runtime errors in modern build pipelines. Learn the technical reasons, migration strategies to union types and const objects, and why the dep
articles.body_html:
TypeScript const Enums Are Deprecated: What to Migrate to and Why the Compiler Team Made the Call

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

TypeScript const enums promised zero-runtime cost for constant values, but they broke isolated module compilation and caused runtime errors downstream. The compiler team deprecated them not because of theoretical purity, but because they caused production failures when developers mixed const enums with modern build tools like esbuild, swc, and Vite. A const enum in a library's .d.ts file becomes a landmine: the consuming project inlines values at compile time but ships code that expects those enum objects to exist at runtime. When versions drift between compile and runtime dependencies, conditionals take the wrong branch and silent data corruption follows.

The problem diagram shows the failure path:

const enum compilation breaks when compiler cannot see declaration file

The solution eliminates compile-time inlining and removes the dependency on cross-module information:

union types with as const provide type safety without runtime dependencies

TypeScript const enum deprecation warning in compiler output

The migration path depends on whether the enum appears in a library or application code. Libraries must remove const enums entirely because they cannot control how downstream consumers compile their code. Application code can migrate incrementally, starting with high-risk modules that interact with external dependencies.

Key Takeaways

  • Const enums fail in isolated module compilation because the compiler cannot access cross-file information to inline values, causing unresolved imports at runtime.
  • The TypeScript team deprecated const enums to prevent version drift bugs where compile-time values differ from runtime values, leading to wrong conditional branches and data corruption.
  • Union types with as const provide equivalent type safety without runtime objects, making them compatible with modern build tools that compile modules in isolation.
  • Libraries shipping .d.ts files with const enums force downstream consumers to disable isolatedModules, breaking compatibility with esbuild, swc, and other fast compilers.
  • The preserveConstEnums compiler option emits runtime objects but defeats the original zero-cost promise and creates inconsistent behavior between development and production builds.

The Technical Problems With Const Enums

Const enums operate by replacing references with literal values at compile time. When the compiler encounters Direction.Up, it substitutes the numeric literal 0 directly into the emitted JavaScript. This inlining removes the enum object from the output entirely, which sounds efficient until modules compile independently.

The TypeScript documentation on enums explains that const enums "are completely removed during compilation" and "members are inlined at use sites." The removal happens because the compiler treats the enum as a macro expansion rather than a runtime value.

const enum inlining requires cross-module visibility to substitute values

The inlining breaks when the compiler processes files in isolation. Modern build tools compile TypeScript modules independently to maximize parallelism. A module that imports a const enum from another file cannot inline the values because it never reads the declaring file. The import statement stays in the output JavaScript, referencing an enum object that was never emitted.

The failure mode appears when libraries publish ambient const enums in declaration files. A library's .d.ts file declares the const enum shape but provides no implementation. The consuming project's compiler sees the declaration and inlines values based on that snapshot. At runtime, the library's JavaScript code contains no enum object because the const modifier stripped it during the library's build. The consuming code executes with hardcoded values that may not match the library's current version.

Version drift amplifies the problem. A project compiles against version 1.2 of a library, inlining Status.Active = 5. The deployment runtime loads version 1.3 where Status.Active changed to 7. The compiled code still checks if (status === 5) but the library now returns 7 for active status. The conditional silently fails and the application continues executing on the wrong path.

The isolatedModules compiler option exists specifically to catch these situations. When enabled, TypeScript rejects code patterns that only work with whole-program compilation. The documentation states that isolatedModules "is fundamentally incompatible with ambient const enums" because inlining requires seeing the enum definition.

Build tools choose isolated module compilation for speed. The TypeScript 5.0 release notes introduced the verbatimModuleSyntax option to make module semantics explicit and predictable across different compilers. The new option removes import elision and treats all module syntax literally, which makes const enum inlining impossible.

The TypeScript team deprecated const enums because they require whole-program knowledge in an ecosystem moving toward isolated compilation. The tradeoff between zero-cost abstractions and compilation speed tilted decisively toward speed when developers started hitting production failures from version drift.

How Const Enums Break in Isolated Module Compilation

The breakage becomes concrete when examining actual compiler output. A const enum in one file and an import in another produces different JavaScript depending on whether the compiler processes them together or separately.

// constants.ts
export const enum Direction {
  Up = 0,
  Down = 1,
  Left = 2,
  Right = 3,
}

// movement.ts
import { Direction } from "./constants";

export function move(direction: Direction): string {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

When TypeScript compiles both files together, the output for movement.ts replaces enum references with literals:

// movement.js (whole-program compilation)
export function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case 0: // Direction.Up
      return "moving up";
    case 1: // Direction.Down
      return "moving down";
    case 2: // Direction.Left
      return "moving left";
    case 3: // Direction.Right
      return "moving right";
  }
}

The constants.ts file emits nothing because the const enum disappears entirely. The JavaScript output contains no Direction object and no export statement. This works only because the compiler inlined the values before generating code.

When a build tool compiles movement.ts in isolation, it cannot inline the values because it never reads constants.ts. The output keeps the import statement:

// movement.js (isolated module compilation)
import { Direction } from "./constants";

export function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

At runtime, the JavaScript engine tries to import Direction from constants.js. That file exports nothing because the const enum was stripped during the library's compilation. The import fails with an unresolved module specifier or imports an undefined value, causing the switch statement to match no cases.

Example of runtime error from const enum in isolated compilation

The isolatedModules documentation calls out this specific failure. The compiler option enables a check that rejects const enum imports from external modules. The error message reads: "Cannot access ambient const enums when the '--isolatedModules' flag is provided."

The ambient qualifier matters. An ambient const enum appears in a declaration file without an implementation. Libraries ship .d.ts files containing const enum declarations, expecting consumers to inline the values. The consumer's compiler sees only the declaration and has no way to verify the values match the library's runtime code.

The fix requires either removing the const modifier to emit a runtime object, or migrating to an alternative that works without cross-file inlining. The next sections cover both migration paths and when to use each one.

Migration Path 1: Union Types With as const

Union types combined with the as const assertion replicate const enum type safety without emitting runtime code. The pattern defines an object with as const to create literal types, then extracts a union type from the object's values.

// Before: const enum
const enum Direction {
  Up = 0,
  Down = 1,
  Left = 2,
  Right = 3,
}

// After: union type with as const
const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
} as const;

type Direction = typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction];

The as const assertion tells the compiler to infer the most specific type possible. Without it, TypeScript widens the type to number. With as const, each property gets its exact literal type: 0, 1, 2, 3. The type extraction typeof Direction[keyof typeof Direction] produces the union 0 | 1 | 2 | 3.

union type extraction flow from const object to type parameter

Functions that previously accepted the enum type now accept the extracted union type. The type safety remains identical:

function move(direction: Direction): string {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

move(Direction.Up); // type-safe
move(Direction.Down); // type-safe
move(5); // error: Argument of type '5' is not assignable to parameter of type '0 | 1 | 2 | 3'

The TypeScript compiler enforces that callers pass only the valid direction values. The compiled JavaScript contains a runtime object with the direction properties, making it compatible with isolated module compilation:

const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
};

function move(direction) {
  switch (direction) {
    case Direction.Up:
      return "moving up";
    case Direction.Down:
      return "moving down";
    case Direction.Left:
      return "moving left";
    case Direction.Right:
      return "moving right";
  }
}

The object exists at runtime, so imports resolve correctly even when modules compile in isolation. The tradeoff is a small runtime cost: the object occupies memory and requires a property access instead of using an immediate literal value. For most applications, the cost disappears in the noise of other object allocations.

String-valued enums migrate the same way:

// Before: string const enum
const enum LogLevel {
  Debug = "DEBUG",
  Info = "INFO",
  Warn = "WARN",
  Error = "ERROR",
}

// After: union type with as const
const LogLevel = {
  Debug: "DEBUG",
  Info: "INFO",
  Warn: "WARN",
  Error: "ERROR",
} as const;

type LogLevel = typeof LogLevel[keyof typeof LogLevel];

The union type becomes "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR", which the compiler treats as distinct literal types. The TypeScript handbook on enums notes that "an object with as const could suffice" for many enum use cases, and this migration proves the point.

The pattern works in libraries because it requires no special compiler behavior. A library exports the const object and the type, and consumers import both normally. No inlining happens and no cross-file dependencies exist. The module system handles the runtime object like any other export.

Migration Path 2: Plain const Objects

When type safety matters less than convenience, a plain const object without type extraction provides a simpler migration. The object still gets as const to freeze its type, but no union type extraction happens.

// Before: const enum
const enum HttpStatus {
  OK = 200,
  Created = 201,
  BadRequest = 400,
  Unauthorized = 401,
  NotFound = 404,
}

// After: plain const object
const HttpStatus = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
} as const;

Functions accept number instead of the specific union type:

function handleResponse(status: number): void {
  if (status === HttpStatus.OK) {
    console.log("Success");
  } else if (status === HttpStatus.NotFound) {
    console.log("Resource not found");
  }
}

The compiler allows any number, not just the defined status codes. This loses type safety but matches the original const enum behavior more closely. Const enums with numeric values did not prevent passing arbitrary numbers either, they just provided autocomplete for the defined constants.

plain const object migration removes type extraction step

The JavaScript output includes the object exactly as written:

const HttpStatus = {
  OK: 200,
  Created: 201,
  BadRequest: 400,
  Unauthorized: 401,
  NotFound: 404,
};

function handleResponse(status) {
  if (status === HttpStatus.OK) {
    console.log("Success");
  } else if (status === HttpStatus.NotFound) {
    console.log("Resource not found");
  }
}

This pattern suits internal application code where the team controls all usage sites. The lack of type constraints speeds up refactoring because changing a value requires updating only the object definition, not every function signature that references it.

Libraries should prefer the union type approach. Exporting a plain object without extracted types gives consumers no guidance about valid values. The autocomplete shows the object properties but the type system accepts anything, leading to runtime errors when callers pass invalid values.

The const object approach also handles computed enum values better than union types. Const enums with expressions become cumbersome to migrate to unions:

// Before: const enum with computed values
const enum Permissions {
  None = 0,
  Read = 1 << 0,
  Write = 1 << 1,
  Execute = 1 << 2,
  ReadWrite = Read | Write,
}

// After: plain const object preserves expressions
const Permissions = {
  None: 0,
  Read: 1 << 0,
  Write: 1 << 1,
  Execute: 1 << 2,
  ReadWrite: (1 << 0) | (1 << 1),
} as const;

Extracting a union type here requires computing the expression results manually (1 | 2 | 4 | 3), which defeats the purpose of the named constants. The plain object keeps the expressions readable and maintains the relationship between combined flags.

Const Enums vs Regular Enums vs Modern Alternatives

The three approaches differ in runtime presence, type safety, and compatibility with modern build tools. The table summarizes the key distinctions:

Feature Const Enum Regular Enum Union Type with as const Plain const Object
Runtime object No Yes Yes Yes
Type safety Compile-time only Full Full None
Isolated modules Breaks Works Works Works
Bundle size impact None Small object Small object Small object
Reverse mapping No Yes No No
Library-safe No Yes Yes Conditional

comparison flowchart showing const enum versus modern alternatives

Regular enums emit a runtime object that supports reverse mapping. Numeric enums create a two-way mapping between names and values:

enum Direction {
  Up,
  Down,
  Left,
  Right,
}

console.log(Direction.Up); // 0
console.log(Direction[0]); // "Up"

The compiled JavaScript contains an immediately invoked function expression that builds the bidirectional object:

var Direction;
(function (Direction) {
  Direction[Direction["Up"] = 0] = "Up";
  Direction[Direction["Down"] = 1] = "Down";
  Direction[Direction["Left"] = 2] = "Left";
  Direction[Direction["Right"] = 3] = "Right";
})(Direction || (Direction = {}));

This flexibility comes with a larger bundle footprint. The generated code uses more bytes than a simple object literal. Most applications never use reverse mapping, making the extra code pure overhead.

Union types with as const provide the same compile-time type safety as enums without the reverse mapping machinery. The object literal approach generates minimal JavaScript and works identically across all compilers. The TypeScript 5.0 release notes mention that the verbatimModuleSyntax option makes module semantics predictable, and union types fit that predictability better than enums with their special compilation rules.

Plain const objects sacrifice type safety for simplicity. They work when the codebase treats the values as documentation rather than constraints. API response status codes often fall into this category because external services return arbitrary numbers anyway.

The migration path depends on the enum's role in the codebase. Enums used as discriminated union tags need full type safety and should become union types. Enums used as named constants can become plain objects. Enums with reverse mapping lookups should stay as regular enums.

What to Do With Existing Const Enum Code

Migrating a codebase with existing const enums requires assessing impact before changing code. The first step identifies where const enums appear and whether they cross module boundaries.

migration decision flowchart for const enum replacement strategy

Search the codebase for const enum declarations and catalog their locations. Distinguish between application-internal enums and enums exported from library packages. Internal enums can migrate gradually. Exported enums require immediate attention because downstream consumers may already be hitting compilation failures.

For libraries, the migration path is strict. Remove all const enums from published declaration files. The TypeScript documentation on const enums explains that const enums in .d.ts files create "subtle implications" and "pitfalls" for consumers. The practical implication is that consumers cannot use isolatedModules if they import your const enums.

The migration steps for a library:

  1. Replace const enum declarations with union types using as const
  2. Export both the const object and the extracted type
  3. Update internal code to use the new types
  4. Bump the major version because the change breaks consumers who directly accessed enum values
  5. Document the migration in the changelog

Application code has more flexibility. The preserveConstEnums compiler option provides a temporary bridge. When enabled, the compiler emits runtime objects for const enums instead of removing them entirely. This makes the code compatible with isolated module compilation while preserving the const enum syntax:

// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "preserveConstEnums": true
  }
}

The output JavaScript now includes the enum object:

const Direction = {
  Up: 0,
  Down: 1,
  Left: 2,
  Right: 3,
};

The const enum keyword becomes equivalent to a regular enum in terms of output, but the TypeScript compiler still inlines references during type checking. This creates an inconsistency where development builds inline values but production builds use the runtime object.

The better approach for application code migrates const enums to union types one module at a time. Start with modules that interact with external dependencies or appear in the critical path. These modules cause the most visible failures when const enums break.

The migration preserves type safety by using the union type extraction pattern. Tests catch any mismatches where code passed invalid values that const enums silently accepted. Strict TypeScript configurations with strict enabled surface these issues immediately.

For large codebases, automated refactoring tools can handle the mechanical transformation. A codemod script searches for const enum declarations, generates the equivalent as const object and type extraction, and updates references throughout the codebase. The TypeScript compiler API provides the parsing and type information needed to build such tools.

The investment in migration pays off in build performance and reliability. Codebases that remove const enums can enable isolatedModules and use faster build tools. The reduction in compilation time often measures in seconds for medium-sized projects and minutes for large monorepos.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still use regular enums without the const modifier?

Yes. Regular enums work correctly with isolated module compilation because they emit runtime objects. The TypeScript compiler team deprecated only const enums due to their specific inlining behavior. Regular enums remain a supported feature with no planned deprecation.

Does preserveConstEnums make const enums safe to use?

No. The preserveConstEnums option emits runtime objects but does not solve the version drift problem. If your library ships .d.ts files with const enums, downstream consumers still inline values at compile time based on your declaration file. The runtime object your library includes may have different values, causing the same silent failures const enums are known for.

Why not just ban const enums with a linter rule?

Linter rules prevent new const enums but do not address existing ones or const enums in dependencies. The TypeScript compiler deprecated const enums to signal that the feature causes real problems and the team will not fix edge cases. Migration to alternatives provides a permanent solution rather than piecemeal prevention.

Will regular enums eventually be deprecated too?

The TypeScript team has not announced plans to deprecate regular enums. The TypeScript handbook still documents enums as a standard feature alongside the as const alternative, giving developers a choice based on their needs. Const enums failed because they broke fundamental module system assumptions, not because enums as a concept are flawed.

How do union types handle bitwise operations like flags?

Union types cannot represent computed values in the type itself, so bitwise flag operations work better with plain const objects. Define the base flags as separate properties and combine them at runtime. The type system sees only the defined properties, not the computed combinations. This limitation makes plain objects more practical than union types for permission flags and similar use cases.

The Future of Enums in TypeScript

The TypeScript compiler team's decision to deprecate const enums reflects a broader shift toward compilation models that prioritize speed and simplicity over optimization tricks. Modern JavaScript bundlers and build tools achieve better performance through parallelization and caching than through aggressive inlining. The zero-runtime-cost promise of const enums mattered more when JavaScript environments were slower and every byte counted.

Union types with as const emerged as the recommended pattern because they align with JavaScript's object literals while providing TypeScript's type safety. The pattern requires no special compiler support and works identically whether the code compiles with tsc, esbuild, swc, or any future compiler. Developers can reason about the code's behavior without understanding const enum inlining rules.

Related posts on TypeScript's evolution cover adjacent deprecation decisions. The TypeScript 6 breaking changes guide discusses other features the compiler team phased out for similar reliability reasons. The TypeScript 6 final JavaScript release explains how new ECMAScript proposals influence TypeScript's feature set. The TypeScript decorators legacy to TC39 migration shows another case where TypeScript deprecated an experimental feature in favor of the standardized alternative.

Const enums served their purpose when build pipelines were simpler and projects rarely mixed compilers. The ecosystem has moved on. The migration to union types or const objects removes a source of subtle bugs and makes TypeScript codebases more portable across different build tools. Teams that complete the migration gain faster build times and fewer production surprises. The const enum deprecation pushes TypeScript toward patterns that scale with modern development workflows rather than fighting against them.
