articles.body_html:
Hello folks, as promised, back with the blog of Next.js file-based routing.

Next.js has one of the most elegant routing systems in the React ecosystem: file-system based routing. Instead of manually declaring routes in a configuration file, the structure of your folders and files is the routing structure. This blog focuses exclusively on the modern App Router (app/ directory) and covers every major routing convention in detail.

Introduction – File-Based Routing & App Router vs Pages Router

Traditionally, you often write something like:

router.get('/blog/:slug', handler)

Next.js flips this model. You create a folder named blog, put a file inside it, and the route appears automatically.

There are two routing systems in Next.js:

  • Pages Router (pages/ directory) – the original system (still fully supported).
  • App Router (app/ directory) – introduced in Next.js 13, built on React Server Components, nested layouts, streaming, and more powerful conventions.

This guide uses the App Router, which is the recommended approach for all new projects.

Core Mental Model

Three rules govern almost everything:

  1. Folders = Route Segments

    Every folder inside app/ becomes a route segment in the URL.

  2. page.tsx (or page.jsx) makes a route public

    A folder without a page.tsx is not a public route. It can still contain nested layouts, components, or other files.

  3. Special files create UI and behavior

    • layout.tsx → shared UI that wraps the segment and all children (can be global or nested)
    • loading.tsx → loading UI
    • error.tsx → error boundary
    • not-found.tsx → 404 UI (can be global or nested)

Folders + Files = URLs

With these rules in mind, let’s explore each routing pattern.

1. Static Routes + Nested Static Routes

Folder structure

app/
├── page.tsx                        → /
├── about/
│   └── page.tsx                    → /about
├── blog/
│   └── page.tsx                    → /blog
└── dashboard/
    ├── page.tsx                    → /dashboard
    ├── analytics/
    │   └── page.tsx                → /dashboard/analytics
    └── settings/
        ├── page.tsx                → /dashboard/settings
        └── profile/
            └── page.tsx            → /dashboard/settings/profile

Static routes are the simplest form: the folder name becomes the exact URL segment. Nesting folders creates nested URLs. Each level can optionally have its own layout.tsx that only wraps that segment and its children.

Key technical notes

  • The root app/page.tsx is required for the homepage (/).
  • A folder without page.tsx is invisible to the router (great for colocation).
  • Layouts nest automatically: root layout → dashboard layout → settings layout.

2. Dynamic Routes (Single Segment)

Folder structure

app/
└── blog/
    ├── page.tsx                    → /blog
    └── [slug]/
        └── page.tsx                → /blog/:slug

A dynamic segment is created by wrapping the folder name in square brackets: [slug]. The value of slug is extracted from the URL and passed to your page.

Accessing the parameter (server component)

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <h1>Blog Post: {slug}</h1>;
}

Key technical notes

  • In recent Next.js versions, params is a Promise — you must await it.
  • Client Components can use the useParams() hook from next/navigation.
  • Use generateStaticParams() to pre-render known dynamic paths at build time (covered later).

3. Multiple Dynamic Route Segments

Folder structure

app/
└── shop/
    └── [category]/
        └── [productId]/
            └── page.tsx            → /shop/:category/:productId

You can stack as many dynamic segments as you need. Each [param] is independent and appears in the params object.

Example

URL params
/shop/electronics/iphone-15 { category: "electronics", productId: "iphone-15" }
/shop/clothing/nike-air { category: "clothing", productId: "nike-air" } 
export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ category: string; productId: string }>;
}) {
  const { category, productId } = await params;
  // fetch product data using both values
}

You can freely mix static and dynamic segments (e.g. /shop/[category]/reviews/[reviewId]).

4. Catch-All Routes

Folder structure

app/
└── docs/
    └── [...slug]/
        └── page.tsx                → /docs/*  (one or more segments)

The [...slug] syntax (ellipsis inside brackets) captures one or more segments as an array. This is introduced because when we don't know about the depth of level in multiple dynamic routes then this is the best option to choose.

URL params.slug
/docs/getting-started ['getting-started']
/docs/api/auth ['api', 'auth']
/docs/a/b/c/d ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']

Important: A regular catch-all does not match the parent path /docs. That would 404 unless you also have a docs/page.tsx.

export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string[] }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <div>Path: {slug.join(' / ')}</div>;
}

5. Optional Catch-All Routes

Folder structure

app/
└── docs/
    └── [[...slug]]/
        └── page.tsx                → /docs  AND  /docs/*

Double square brackets [[...slug]] make the catch-all optional. It now also matches the route with zero additional segments means it solves the problem of catch-all-routes also.

URL params.slug
/docs undefined
/docs/getting-started ['getting-started']
/docs/api/auth ['api', 'auth']

This pattern is extremely useful for documentation sites, knowledge bases, or any UI that needs a root view plus arbitrary depth.

Always handle the undefined case in your component.

Important: Don't ever use both the catch all routes and optional catch all routes together not under the same folder. Either use first one or the second one; but not together under same folder.

export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug?: string[] }>;
}) {
  const { slug } = await params;
  return <div>Path: {slug ? slug.join('/') : '(no slug — matched /page itself)'}</div>;
}

6. Route Groups (+ Private Folders)

Folder structure

app/
├── (marketing)/
│   ├── page.tsx                    → /
│   ├── about/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /about
│   ├── pricing/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /pricing
│   └── layout.tsx                  // marketing layout only
├── (shop)/
│   ├── products/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /products
│   ├── cart/
│   │   └── page.tsx                → /cart
│   └── layout.tsx                  // shop layout only
├── (dashboard)/
│   ├── layout.tsx                  // dashboard layout
│   └── settings/
│       └── page.tsx                → /settings
└── layout.tsx                      // root layout

Route groups are created by wrapping a folder name in parentheses: (marketing). The parentheses and the name inside them never appear in the URL. They exist purely for organization and for applying different layouts to different sets of routes. If we don't want to show the folder structure in the route/URL itself, then we will use this.

Common use cases

  • Separate marketing pages from authenticated dashboard pages
  • Apply different root layouts
  • Organize by team or feature without polluting the URL

Private folders (related convention)

Prefix any folder with an underscore (_components, _lib, _utils). These folders and everything inside them are completely ignored by the router — perfect for colocation.

Important rules

  • Two different route groups cannot resolve to the same URL path (build-time error).
  • Navigating between routes that use different root layouts triggers a full page load.

Practical Tips

Mixing conventions

You can combine everything freely:

app/
└── (shop)/
    └── [category]/
        └── [...slug]/
            └── page.tsx

generateStaticParams

For dynamic and catch-all routes you often want static generation:

// app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx
export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const posts = await getAllPosts();
  return posts.map((post) => ({ slug: post.slug }));
}

Layouts interaction

  • Layouts wrap their children and persist across navigations within the same segment.
  • A layout inside a route group only applies to routes inside that group.
  • Root layout is required (unless you intentionally create multiple root layouts via route groups).

Common pitfalls

  • Forgetting that a folder needs a page.tsx to be public.
  • Conflicting paths between two route groups.
  • Not awaiting params in newer Next.js versions.
  • Expecting a regular catch-all [...slug] to match the parent path.
  • Putting business logic or shared components directly in route folders instead of using private folders or a top-level components/ directory.

Conclusion & Further Reading

File-based routing in the App Router is both powerful and surprisingly simple once the core mental model clicks: folders define segments, page.tsx makes them public, and special naming conventions ([], [...], [[...]], ()) give you dynamic behavior and organization.

Master these patterns and you can model almost any URL structure cleanly while keeping your project organized and performant.

Official documentation

  • Defining Routes
  • Dynamic Route Segments
  • Route Groups
  • Project Structure

Happy routing!

articles.title: Figma: 'line-height: auto' não se traduz sozinho no Browser
articles.description: Se você já exportou um design do Figma e o espaçamento entre linhas "quebrou" não ficou perfeito como...
articles.body_html:
Se você já exportou um design do Figma e o espaçamento entre linhas "quebrou" não ficou perfeito como o seu perfeccionismo de pixel perfect queria no navegador, a explicação é pra você acalmar o seu suricato mental que reclama toda vez que isso acontece.

Vamos salvar 5 minutos do seu dia? Ok.

TL;DR

Contexto auto / normal
Figma Métricas intrínsecas da fonte (engine própria)
Navegador Métricas intrínsecas da fonte (engine do browser)
Resultado Pode divergir em 1–3px

Aos designers: defina valores explícitos. Seu dev agradece.

Agora falando mais sério, o problema:

No Figma, o campo de Line Height vem com a opção Auto selecionada por padrão. Parece inofensivo, até gentil! Mas esse "Auto" não é igual ao normal do CSS. Daí quando você é chato, aqueles pixels incomodam bastante.

O Auto do Figma usa as métricas verticais intrínsecas da fonte (hhea/OS/2 no .ttf/.otf), definidas pelo designer tipográfico. Cada fonte tem um valor diferente: uma pode ter ~1.2× o font-size, outra ~1.4×.

Vamos pegar a fonte Montserrat por exemplo. Com size 16px, o leading dela é 20px. Aliás, leading é o termo correto para essa parte técnica da tipografia.

No navegador, o line-height: normal (que é o default) também usa métricas da fonte, mas cada engine de texto resolve de forma ligeiramente diferente. Resultado: o que você vê no Figma não é pixel-perfect no Chrome, Firefox ou Safari. E se você, como eu, tem o hábito de usar um reset para line-height: 1, também vai quebrar.

Tá, mas e aí, como descobrir o leading real no Figma

O Figma não exibe o valor numérico do Auto. Mas dá pra puxar de um jeito muito simples que me fez sentir besta de tão óbvio:

  1. Crie um texto de uma linha só na fonte e tamanho desejado.
  2. Deixe o Line Height em Auto.
  3. Olhe a altura da camada de texto no painel de propriedades — esse é o leading em px. O height. Simples assim.

Na prática

O projeto com consistência entre design e código:

  • Defina um line-height fixo (em px ou em unidade relativa) no Figma. Ex.: 1.5 ou 24px pra fonte de 16px.
  • Evite depender do Auto se o dev vai reproduzir o layout manualmente... Ou se a sua IA não é treinada para pensar no leading.

Espero ter resolvido uma coceira de perfeccionismo por aí.

articles.title: Folio.AspNetCore — an embeddable OpenAPI UI for ASP.NET Core
articles.description: Most OpenAPI UIs for ASP.NET Core work the same way: you generate a spec, then host a separate set of...
articles.body_html:
Most OpenAPI UIs for ASP.NET Core work the same way: you generate a spec,
then host a separate set of static files to render it. That's fine until
you want it to just... work, out of the box, offline, without another
build step in your pipeline.

I spent the last few months building Folio.AspNetCore — an OpenAPI
documentation and testing UI that ships entirely as a NuGet package. No
static files to host yourself, no CDN dependencies, no separate build
step. Install the package, point it at your OpenAPI document, done.

dotnet add package Folio.AspNetCore

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddOpenApi();

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapOpenApi();

app.UseFolio(options =>
{
    options.SpecUrl = "/openapi/v1.json";
});

app.Run();

That's the whole setup. Open /folio and you get the full UI.

What you get

Browsing

  • Endpoint list, grouped and searchable, generated straight from the spec
  • A full, separately-browsable model/schema catalog — not just inline types buried in each endpoint
  • Markdown-rendered descriptions (from the spec's own description fields)

A real request builder, not a raw JSON textarea

Parameters and request body fields get the right control for their
schema type — text inputs, number steppers, boolean toggles, enum
dropdowns, date pickers, nested object/array editors. You can still drop
into raw JSON if you want to.

Live code generation, in six languages

Every request gets an equivalent code snippet — cURL, JavaScript
(fetch), Python (requests), C# (HttpClient), Go (net/http),
PowerShell (Invoke-RestMethod) — updated live as you fill in the form,
before you even hit Send. Syntax-highlighted too.

Per-endpoint role visibility

If your endpoints use [Authorize(Roles = "...")], Folio shows exactly
which roles are required, right in the sidebar and on the endpoint page —
read directly from your routing metadata via EndpointDataSource.
Nothing to configure, nothing duplicated: it's a live mirror of what your
code already declares.

app.MapPost("/api/items", CreateItem)
    .RequireAuthorization(new AuthorizeAttribute { Roles = "Admin" });

That attribute alone is enough — Folio picks it up automatically.

Environments, headers, auth

  • Switch between base URLs (local/staging/prod) without touching code, or import servers[] straight from the spec
  • Global headers (e.g. an API key) applied to every request, separate from per-endpoint headers
  • A dedicated modal for the spec's own security schemes (apiKey, HTTP Bearer/Basic)

Gating the docs themselves

Two ways to put a login in front of the UI:

// Integrate with auth you already have
app.UseFolio(options =>
{
    options.AuthorizationPolicy = "FolioAccess";
    options.LogoutUrl = "/account/logout";
});

// Or a self-contained cookie-based login, zero existing auth required
builder.Services.AddFolioAuth(options =>
{
    options.Users = builder.Configuration.GetSection("Users").Get<List<FolioUser>>() ?? [];
});

app.UseFolioAuth();
app.UseFolio(options => options.SpecUrl = "/openapi/v1.json");

Fine-grained control over what's shown

Every major UI element — the execute button, code generator, role
badges, schema viewer, environment switcher, and more — can be toggled
independently:

app.UseFolio(options =>
{
    options.ShowTryItOut = false; // read-only docs deployment, say
});

...or bound from appsettings.json explicitly (Folio never reads config
on its own — this only runs if you call it):

app.UseFolio((context, options) =>
{
    options.ReadFrom.Configuration(context.Configuration, "Folio");
});

How it's built

It's a classic ASP.NET Core middleware (app.Use...), not endpoint
routing. The UI's HTML/CSS/JS live as embedded resources, served through
a real StaticFileMiddleware on top of ManifestEmbeddedFileProvider —
proper ETag/Last-Modified/conditional requests, not hand-rolled file
serving.

Multi-targets .NET 6 through 9.

Try it 

dotnet add package Folio.AspNetCore
  • GitHub: https://github.com/bekov0004/Folio.AspNetCore
  • NuGet: https://www.nuget.org/packages/Folio.AspNetCore
  • Wiki (getting started, auth setup, FAQ): https://github.com/bekov0004/Folio.AspNetCore/wiki

Feedback and issues welcome — especially if something's missing for your
use case.

articles.title: 10 AI Terms Every Developer Should Know to Build Better Systems
articles.description: In my last speech, I wanted the audience to leave with something they could use beyond a particular...
articles.body_html:
In my last speech, I wanted the audience to leave with something they could use beyond a particular AI tool.

So I focused on how to think with AI.

While building ReThynk AI, one lesson has become central to my thinking: start with the problem. Understand what needs to happen, who needs it, and how you will know whether your solution works.

Technical knowledge becomes valuable when it helps us answer those questions.

That is why I want developers to understand these ten terms. Each gives you a way to examine your application, identify a weakness, and make a better decision.

Let us connect them through one example: building an AI customer-support assistant.

1. Context window

The context window is the amount of information a model can work with during a response, measured in tokens. Its capacity must accommodate the relevant input and generated output, subject to the model’s limits. It is different from permanent memory.

Imagine your support assistant needs the customer’s question, conversation history, and refund policy. Those compete for space alongside instructions and tool results.

A larger window gives you more room. You still need to decide what deserves that room.

2. Context engineering

Context engineering means selecting, organizing, and maintaining the information available to the model as it works. This includes instructions, documents, conversation history, and tool results.

For our assistant, loading every policy document could introduce outdated or irrelevant information. Selecting the current policy for the customer’s region gives it a more useful starting point.

My question here is simple: Have I given the system what it needs to make this particular decision?

3. Embeddings

Embeddings represent information as numerical vectors. Suitable embedding models allow us to compare text by semantic similarity, which is useful for search, clustering, and retrieval.

A customer writes, “My parcel never arrived.” Your documentation calls this a “missing delivery.” Embedding-based search can help connect the two despite their different wording.

However, a similar document can still be the wrong document. You must also consider details such as product, region, and policy date.

4. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG

RAG retrieves relevant information and supplies it to a model to help generate an answer. It connects generation with external sources such as documents or databases.

Our assistant could retrieve a delivery policy before explaining the available options.

That sounds straightforward, but there are two questions to investigate: did retrieval find the right information, and did the model use it correctly?

Connecting a document store is the beginning of that work.

5. Tool calling

Tool calling allows a model to request an external function using structured arguments. For custom functions, your application executes the function and returns its result to the model.

For example, the assistant might request:

get_order_status(order_id="12345")

Your application must check whether the customer can access that order before executing the request.

The model can propose an action. Your software remains responsible for enforcing permissions and validating inputs.

6. Workflows and agents

In Anthropic’s architectural distinction, workflows follow predefined code paths, while agents dynamically direct their processes and tool use. Different products may use these labels differently, so the underlying behavior matters.

A support workflow might always check the order, retrieve the policy, and draft a response.

An agent might decide which investigation to perform next based on what it discovers.

When building, I would ask how much flexibility the problem requires. A predictable process can be easier to inspect, test, and maintain.

7. Model Context Protocol, or MCP

MCP standardizes how AI applications connect with capabilities exposed by servers, including tools, resources, and prompts. Its architecture separates the host application, clients, and servers.

For our support assistant, an MCP server could expose order-search tools or policy resources.

This helps define the connection. You still need to design access controls, tool behavior, and error handling.

Understanding the protocol should help you build clearer interfaces between your AI application and the systems it uses.

8. Evaluations, or evals

Evaluations are structured checks of how a system performs on representative tasks. For a RAG application, useful dimensions include correctness, relevance, completeness, and whether the response is supported by its supplied context.

Our assistant needs test cases for missing deliveries, conflicting policies, unavailable order data, and questions it cannot answer.

My Six Sigma background makes this especially meaningful to me. Before improving a process, we need a clear definition of acceptable performance.

A convincing demonstration gives us something to investigate. Evaluation gives us evidence across cases.

9. Observability

Observability helps us understand a system’s behavior through telemetry such as traces, metrics, and logs. A trace can follow a request through multiple operations.

Suppose our assistant gives a poor answer after taking fifteen seconds. We need to discover where the time went, which documents were retrieved, and whether a tool failed.

For AI applications, I would track the relevant retrieval, model, and tool steps while protecting sensitive customer information.

We can improve more effectively when we can locate the failure.

10. Idempotency

An idempotent operation can be repeated without producing additional effects beyond the intended first operation. This matters when requests are retried after timeouts or interrupted connections.

Imagine a refund succeeds, but the response never reaches the assistant. It retries.

The system should recognize the same logical refund request and avoid issuing another payment. Implementing that requires coordination with the service performing the action.

A retry is a small technical detail until it changes someone’s account balance.

These concepts belong together.

Context engineering determines what the model sees. Retrieval supplies information. Tools connect it to actions. Workflows or agents coordinate the work. Evaluations check performance, observability helps explain behavior, and idempotency helps make retries safe.

When I speak about thinking with AI, this is part of what I mean: understanding enough of the whole system to ask better questions.

Choose one AI project you are building. Trace a single user request through it.

Where could it retrieve the wrong information, take an unauthorized action, or repeat an operation?

Share the term you want me to explore next, and the problem you are trying to solve with it.

articles.title: What is your role in your agentic setup?
articles.description: A few weeks ago I wrote about how I stopped coding and started orchestrating. Ten terminal tabs,...
articles.body_html:
A few weeks ago I wrote about how I stopped coding and started orchestrating. Ten terminal tabs, three startups, me pressing Enter all day. Then I moved the whole setup to a Mac mini, put an orchestrator agent in charge of a pool of workers (coding agents, a design agent, a DevOps agent, an accounting agent), and went from 1 PR a day to 22.

I called myself an orchestrator. Then a manager of orchestrators. Both titles felt a bit grand for what I was actually doing.

With my daughter a couple of weeks away, I started re-reading my favorite book of Adler psychology, the courage to be happy. One idea stuck: the job of a parent is not to do things for the child, or to tell the child what to do all day. The job is to educate the child so that one day they can fend for themselves.

I read that sentence with my phone on my knee and the orchestrator asking me for the third time that morning whether it could run a migration.

And it clicked. I had the wrong job title all along.

You are not a product manager. You are an educator.

The industry has settled on two words for what humans do with AI agents: product manager and orchestrator. I think both are wrong, and the wrong word leads to the wrong setup.

A product manager writes a ticket, hands it over, and waits for the result. That is how I used my first workers. Every task started from zero. The agent didn't know my codebase conventions, didn't know we deploy with Kamal, and didn't know I hate service objects with more than one public method. So I wrote it all in the ticket. Every. Single. Time.

An orchestrator is worse. An orchestrator decides every move. That is the setup that turned me into a finger pressing Enter. The agents had no autonomy because I had given them none. I was not slow because the AI was slow; I was slow because I was the bottleneck in every decision.

An educator does something different. Adler is careful with the word: a teacher transmits facts; an educator shapes a person who can live on their own. An educator spends time up front so that later the child does not need them. You explain how the world works, you let them try, you correct, and you step back a bit more each time. The goal of the educator is to become unnecessary.

That is exactly what happened with my orchestrator without me noticing. It did not become useful because I gave it better tickets. It became useful because it knows how I work, what security I need, which decisions it can take alone and which ones to escalate to me. I educated it, mostly by accident.

Once I saw it as education, I started doing it on purpose.

Human knowledge, and AI knowledge

Adler makes a distinction I found useful. There is the knowledge you learn at school (maths, history, how to read), and there is a second kind of knowledge nobody writes an exam about: the shared rules for living with other people. You stop at a red light. You don’t talk in the cinema. You bring something when you are invited to dinner. Nobody is born with this. Every generation learns it from the previous one, and a child who does not learn it cannot function in society no matter how smart they are.

AI agents are in exactly that situation. The model is the smartest kid in the class. It knows Rails better than I do, it has read more Postgres documentation than any human alive. What it does not know is how to live in my house.

I started calling this AI knowledge: the basic set of rules an agent needs to perform tasks and fulfill its goals inside a specific environment. Not model weights, not prompts. The equivalent of knowing where the traffic lights are.

For my setup, AI knowledge looks like this:

Where things live: which repo is which startup, where the Obsidian vault is, which folder is the accounting drive.

How we ship: branch naming, PR size, what a green pipeline means, that nothing deploys on Friday evening Bali time.

What is dangerous: which commands need a human, which tables you never touch in production, what counts as a customer-facing change.

Who does what: the orchestrator dispatches, coding workers write and test, the design agent owns the UI, the DevOps agent deploys and monitors, the accounting agent does the books, I do strategy and the final say on money.

What already happened: decisions from co-founder meetings, bugs we already fixed last year, features we tried and killed.

None of this is in the model. All of it is in markdown files, a vault, and a handful of CLAUDE.md files that I keep adding to every time an agent does something that makes me say “no, not like that”.

The test is simple. If a brand new worker spins up tomorrow, can it fend for itself in my codebase with zero instructions from me? If the answer is no, I have not finished educating it. I have just written a very long ticket.

Knowledge only survives if it gets passed on

Human knowledge persists for one reason: people pass it forward. My parents taught me, I will teach my daughter; she will teach hers. Nobody re-derives the rules of society from scratch every morning.

Agents, by default, do exactly that. Every session starts from zero. Every worker is a newborn. Whatever a worker learned yesterday (that the test suite is flaky on the mailer specs, that the staging database has a weird extension) dies with its context window.

So the second part of the educator’s job is to make sure the knowledge outlives the one who learned it.

In practice, this means agents educating agents. Here is how it works in my setup:

A worker finishes a task and writes what it learned into the vault: a gotcha, a decision, a convention it discovered by breaking something.

The orchestrator reviews it. If it is a real rule and not a one-off, it goes into the shared AI knowledge. If it is noise, it gets dropped.

The next worker that touches that area reads it before starting.

I am not in that loop. That is the point. If I were the only channel through which knowledge moves between agents, I would be back to being the bottleneck, just with a nicer job title.

The nice side effect: when the orchestrator stops me from building a feature we already tried and killed last year, that is not the orchestrator being smart. That is a worker from eight months ago educating a worker from today, with me doing nothing.

What a well-educated agent looks like

Adler says a well-educated child has two things: they can take care of themselves, and they can live in harmony with others. I have found no better definition of a good agent.

1. Self-reliance

The agent can get from a task to a merged PR inside my environment without asking me anything. It knows where to look, how to run the tests, how to deploy, when to stop. The number I track for this is interruptions per task. When I started, it was 10 to 15 “allow this command?” per worker. Today the orchestrator absorbs almost all of them and escalates maybe one real decision a day to me.

This is also the one that lets me close the laptop. An agent that cannot fend for itself needs a human at the keyboard. An agent that can needs a Mac mini and a UPS.

2. Harmony with the environment

This is the one most people skip, and it is where agents do the most damage. A self-reliant agent with no sense of the environment is a toddler with a credit card. Very capable, very fast, zero awareness of what is around it.

Harmony means three things in my setup:

  1. Not recreating what already exists. The worker checks the vault and the codebase before writing a new service, a new helper, a new landing page section. The number of duplicated utility classes I had before this rule was embarrassing.

  2. Calling the right tool when needed. If there is a connector for Gmail, use it. If there is a script that generates invoices, run it, do not re-implement it in Ruby from scratch because you can. The right tool includes other agents: a coding worker that hits an accounting question hands it to the accounting agent; it does not improvise Singapore tax law. A worker that needs a new screen asks the design agent, it does not invent its own button style.

  3. Operating in sync with everyone else. Workers run in parallel. Thirty of them on a good night. One worker rewriting the User model while another one is adding a column to it is the agent version of two kids fighting over the same toy. The orchestrator’s job is to sequence them, and each worker’s job is to check what is in flight before it starts.

Self-reliance without harmony gives you fast chaos. Harmony without self-reliance gives you a polite agent that asks permission for everything. You need both, and you only get both by educating the agent, not by writing better tickets.

In Summary

If you take one thing from this post: stop asking “how do I write a better prompt” and start asking “what does this agent need to know to live here without me”.

Your role with AI is not product manager and not orchestrator. It is an educator, in Adler’s sense: someone whose job is to become unnecessary.

AI knowledge is the set of shared rules an agent needs to fend for itself in your environment. It lives in your repo and your vault, not in the model.

Knowledge persists better if agents pass it to other agents instead of simple .md files. If you are the only channel, you are the bottleneck.

A well-educated agent is self-reliant and in harmony with its environment. It does not rebuild what exists; it calls the right tool, and it stays in sync with the other agents.

Now, let’s educate.

Dani,

articles.title: Desktops have SQLite. Servers have Postgres. Now, the browser finally has WebDB — Introducing WebDB
articles.description: How the pain of IndexedDB and bloated WASM ports led me to build a ~19KB browser-native relational database engine.
articles.body_html:
Stop shipping multi-megabyte desktop databases to the browser—the Web finally has its own DB.

If you’ve ever built an offline-first or local-first web application, you already know the storage struggle. Everything starts out fine when you're just caching a few JSON objects. Then, real product requirements kick in: you need to join orders with customers, filter by multiple conditions, calculate totals, paginate results, and keep two open browser tabs in sync without corrupting data.

At that point, you have two choices—and both hurt.

Option 1: The IndexedDB Boilerplate Trap

You start with raw IndexedDB (or a thin wrapper around it). Pretty quickly, you realize IndexedDB isn't a relational database. Want to join two tables? You’re writing manual JavaScript loops and merging cursors in memory. Want a compound filter with sorting and pagination? You’re fighting key ranges and writing dozens of lines of imperative code for what should have been a 3-line query.

Option 2: The Heavy Desktop WASM Port

Frustrated with IndexedDB, you reach for SQLite WASM or PGlite. Now you have real relational queries, which feels great—until you look at the trade-offs:

  1. Massive bundles: You're shipping a 1 MB to 5 MB+ WebAssembly binary designed for desktop filesystems just to store data in a browser tab.
  2. Server header headaches: To get fast synchronous file access in a Worker, you need SharedArrayBuffer, which forces you to add strict COOP and COEP isolation headers to your server—instantly breaking third-party scripts, embeds, and auth popups.
  3. Wasted CPU cycles: Your JavaScript code builds a query, serializes it into a SQL text string, crosses the WASM boundary, and hands it to a multi-megabyte C SQL lexer and AST parser just to tokenize that string back into bytecode instructions.

After hitting this wall one too many times while building offline-capable apps, I asked a simple question: What if we built a relational database engine natively for the browser from scratch?

Today, I’m really excited to launch WebDB.

Rethinking the Architecture: Direct-to-Bytecode

Desktop databases need a SQL text parser because queries come over a network socket as raw strings. In the browser, your application code and your database live in the exact same runtime. Why are we serializing objects into strings just to parse them back again?

WebDB eliminates the middleman entirely:

  • Legacy WASM Ports (4 Stages): JS Query / ORM ➔ SQL String Serialization ➔ C SQL Lexer & AST Parser (+1.5 MB bloat) ➔ WASM Execution
  • WebDB (2 Stages): Fluent TypeScript Query Builder ➔ Direct VDBE Binary Bytecode (< 0.05ms)

Because WebDB compiles fluent TypeScript AST directly into compact binary opcodes (OP_INDEX_SCAN, OP_RESULT_ROW, etc.), we don't need to bundle a massive C string parser.

The result? A full relational engine—with B+Tree indexes, joins, aggregates, subqueries, and crash-proof ACID transactions—inside a ~19 KB gzipped WebAssembly core (~51 KB raw), with a pure JS fallback included.

What Makes WebDB Different?

  • ~19 KB Gzipped WASM Core: Around 95% smaller than typical desktop SQLite or Postgres WASM ports.
  • Up to 8.7x Faster than Official SQLite WASM: Skipping SQL string parsing and Emscripten Asyncify stack-unwinding makes in-memory and indexed workloads significantly faster.
  • Zero COOP/COEP Server Headers: Works out of the box on any static host or CDN without breaking your page isolation.
  • Native Async Virtual File System (VFS): Suspends cleanly on 4 KB page faults over OPFS and IndexedDB. You can even query multi-gigabyte read-only databases hosted on S3 or a CDN via HTTP Range: bytes=X-Y requests without downloading the whole file.
  • Crash-Proof ACID & WAL: Write-Ahead Logging with IEEE 802.3 CRC32 checksums on every 4 KB page prevents corruption when users suddenly close a tab. Multi-tab readers and writers coordinate automatically via navigator.locks.
  • 16-Byte Binary UUIDv7 & ULID: Packs UUIDs into 16 raw bytes (58% smaller than 36-char strings) for fast, zero-fragmentation B+Tree inserts.

How to Use WebDB

1. Define a Schema & Run Relational Queries

No SQL strings to escape. You get full TypeScript autocompletion for schemas, composite B+Tree indexes, JOINs, GROUP BY, HAVING, and aggregates:

// 1. Define relational schema with typed binary columns & B+Tree indexes
await db.createTable("orders", [
  { name: "id", type: "UUID", primaryKey: true }, // Packed into 16 raw bytes
  { name: "customer_id", type: "UUID", notNull: true },
  { name: "status", type: "TEXT", notNull: true },
  { name: "total", type: "FLOAT64", notNull: true },
]);

await db.createIndex("orders", ["status", "total"]);

// 2. Fluent relational query with JOINs, aggregates & filtering
const topCustomers = await db
  .from("orders")
  .join("customers", "orders.customer_id", "=", "customers.id")
  .select("customers.name as customer")
  .sum("orders.total", "lifetimeValue")
  .count("*", "orderCount")
  .where("orders.status", "=", "paid")
  .groupBy("customers.name")
  .having("lifetimeValue", ">=", 500)
  .orderBy("lifetimeValue", "desc")
  .limit(10)
  .toArray();

If you ever want to see what the cost-based query planner is doing under the hood, just call .explain() on any query to inspect the generated VDBE bytecode instructions directly.

2. Reactive Live Queries (React, Vue, Angular & Plain JS)

One of the most annoying parts of offline apps is wiring manual event buses around database writes so your UI knows when to re-render.

WebDB ships with isolated framework subpaths (under 1 KB gzipped each) that automatically inspect your query AST—including JOINs and subqueries. When a relevant table mutates in the current tab, a Web Worker, or another open browser tab (via BroadcastChannel), your UI updates automatically:

import { useLiveQuery } from "@ahmadmoussawi/webdb/react";

export function OrderDashboard({ status }: { status: string }) {
  // Automatically tracks 'orders' AND joined 'customers' table!
  const { data: orders, isLoading } = useLiveQuery(
    () =>
      db
        .from("orders")
        .join("customers", "orders.customer_id", "=", "customers.id")
        .where("orders.status", "=", status)
        .orderBy("orders.id", "desc"),
    [status],
    { initialData: [] }
  );

  // Mutating 'orders' (here or in another tab) automatically updates the UI!
  const markPaid = (id: string) =>
    db.from("orders").where("id", "=", id).update({ status: "paid" });

  if (isLoading) return <p>Loading live orders...</p>;
  return <OrderTable rows={orders} onMarkPaid={markPaid} />;
}

Performance Benchmarks (5,000 Rows In-Memory)

Because WebDB compiles TypeScript directly into binary opcodes and avoids C parser overhead, both the ~19 KB WASM engine and even the pure JS fallback beat official SQLite WASM (:memory:) across common relational workloads (tested on a MacBook Pro M1 Max):

Workload Scenario WebDB (WASM) WebDB (Pure JS) SQLite WASM Speedup vs SQLite
Range Filter Scan 1,091.7 ops/s 444.0 ops/s 125.9 ops/s 8.7x faster
Bulk Batch Insert 359,152 ops/s 301,932 ops/s 156,576 ops/s 2.3x faster
Batch Point Lookups 334,448 ops/s 234,192 ops/s 148,148 ops/s 2.3x faster
Indexed 2-Table JOIN 755.3 ops/s 494.6 ops/s 440.1 ops/s 1.7x faster
Filter + Sort + Limit 2,381.0 ops/s 681.7 ops/s 1,483.7 ops/s 1.6x faster

Don't just take my numbers for it—you can run the live benchmark suite on your own machine here.

Try It in Your Browser (Studio IDE)

To make debugging local databases easier, I also built the WebDB Studio Playground.

Right in your browser, you can write queries with full autocompletion, inspect raw binary 4 KB slotted pages in real time, visualize B+Tree structures, and even share live compressed .webdb.gz databases via URL.

Links & Resources

WebDB is completely open-source under the MIT license. If you’ve ever felt the friction of building offline-first or local-first web apps, I’d love for you to try it out, break it, and let me know what you think!

  • Website & Documentation: https://webdb.dev/
  • Live Studio IDE Playground: https://webdb.dev/playground/
  • In-Browser Benchmarks: https://webdb.dev/benchmark/
  • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ahmad-moussawi/webdb (If you find it useful, a ⭐ on GitHub helps a ton!)

What's been your biggest headache when dealing with client-side storage in the browser? Let me know in the comments!

articles.title: You're Blocking Scroll by Default. `passive: true` Fixes It.
articles.description: Every touch and wheel listener you add can make the browser wait before it scrolls — because it has to check whether you'll call preventDefault(). `passive: true` tells it you won't, and scrolling stops waiting on your code.
articles.body_html:
A teammate scrolled the product list on their phone and said it felt "sticky" — not broken, just a little behind, like the page was thinking about it before it moved. On a laptop trackpad it was perfectly smooth. Same code, same list, same 12-line scroll handler that did almost nothing: check scrollY, toggle a "back to top" button.

Twelve lines. Nothing in it that should cost more than a millisecond. And yet, on a phone, every scroll felt like it had a half-beat of drag.

The fix that didn't fix it

The obvious read is "the handler is too slow," so that's where the first hour went:

list.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
  backToTop.hidden = list.scrollTop < 400;
});

Wait — not even scroll. The actual listener was on touchmove, added so the button could react mid-gesture instead of waiting for the scroll to settle:

list.addEventListener("touchmove", () => {
  backToTop.hidden = list.scrollTop < 400;
});

That one line is the whole bug, and nothing in it looks dangerous. We debounced it. We memoized the scroll position. We moved the class toggle behind requestAnimationFrame. Chrome DevTools' performance panel kept showing the same thing after every change: a yellow "Rendering" block sitting before the scroll could start, not after the handler ran.

Before you keep reading — what do you think the browser was actually waiting for?

It wasn't waiting for the handler to be fast. It was waiting to find out whether the handler would call preventDefault().

Why a touchmove listener can freeze a scroll that never gets cancelled

touchmove, touchstart, and wheel are special. Any listener for one of them is allowed to call event.preventDefault() and cancel the browser's default action — in this case, cancel the scroll itself, mid-gesture. A custom image-zoom gesture, a swipe-to-dismiss card, a "no, don't scroll past this point" lock — all of those work by listening to one of these events and vetoing the browser's plan.

The browser doesn't know in advance that your handler isn't one of those. So by default it plays it safe: run the handler first, check event.defaultPrevented, and only then move the page. Your handler reads scrollY and sets .hidden — completely harmless — but the browser can't see that from the outside. It has to ask.

That ask is synchronous, and it happens on the main thread. If the main thread is busy with literally anything else at that instant — a re-render, a timer, a layout recalculation — the scroll waits behind it. Debouncing the handler doesn't help, because the delay isn't the handler's duration. It's the fact that scrolling is gated on the handler returning at all, every single time it fires.

This is exactly what Lighthouse is flagging when it tells you a page "does not use passive listeners to improve scrolling performance." It isn't measuring your code's speed. It's measuring whether you've told the browser it's allowed to stop asking.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The one-line fix

addEventListener takes a third argument beyond the usual boolean-for-capture — an options object with a passive flag:

list.addEventListener("touchmove", () => {
  backToTop.hidden = list.scrollTop < 400;
}, { passive: true });

{ passive: true } is a promise: this listener will never call preventDefault(). The browser takes you at your word, stops waiting, and starts scrolling the instant the gesture begins — on the compositor thread, independent of whatever your handler is doing. The handler still runs, still takes however long it takes, but scrolling no longer holds its breath for the answer.

Break that promise and call preventDefault() inside a passive listener anyway, and nothing happens — the call is silently ignored. Chrome and Firefox log a console warning telling you so; Safari doesn't, so don't count on the console to catch the mistake for you. There's no partial credit. A listener is either allowed to cancel the gesture, or it isn't, and passive is you choosing which.

Try scrolling the list below with the toggle off, then on — same handler, same cost, very different feel.

"Isn't this already the default?"

Sort of, and that's the trap. A few browsers quietly mark some touch listeners passive on their own — but only in specific cases (certain root-level targets, specific event types), and the exact cases differ by engine and have changed over time as each one shipped its own optimization. Relying on an undocumented default that varies by browser and by which element you attached to is not a strategy. It's a bet.

The one-line fix works everywhere, on every engine, whether or not that engine happens to be feeling generous today:

list.addEventListener("touchmove", handler, { passive: true });
list.addEventListener("wheel", handler, { passive: true });

Add it to every touchstart, touchmove, or wheel listener where you genuinely never call preventDefault() — scroll-position trackers, infinite-scroll triggers, analytics pings, "show the nav on scroll up" toggles, if you've wired them to one of those three events. That's most of them. (A plain scroll listener doesn't need this at all — scroll events are never cancelable, so the browser was never waiting on them in the first place.) The only time you can't use { passive: true } is when the listener sometimes needs to cancel the gesture — a custom swipe handler, a drag-to-reorder list, a pinch-zoom lock. In that case, leaving it non-passive is correct, not an oversight — you're keeping the veto because you actually use it.

The list, scrolling again

Back-to-top button, 12 lines, one options object added. The teammate who first noticed the stutter scrolled the same list on the same phone and didn't say anything — which, for a performance fix, is exactly the review you want. Nobody writes a bug report about something that just works.

Go check one scroll handler in your own codebase right now — does it call preventDefault() anywhere? If the honest answer is no, it's missing one argument. What's the oldest scroll listener in your code that's never had { passive: true } added — and do you know whether it blocks anything?
