articles.title: An AI Testing Presentation Became the Final Push for Organizational Change at My Company
articles.description: From a multi-agent testing experiment to a broader discussion about how engineering teams should...
articles.body_html:
From a multi-agent testing experiment to a broader discussion about how engineering teams should evolve in the age of AI.

At first, I simply wanted to share an AI-powered automated testing system I had been working on.

The system could already understand requirements, generate test cases, interact with web browsers and mobile apps, identify defects, and connect bug fixing with regression testing. I expected the session to focus on how AI could improve testing efficiency.

But during our internal session on November 5, 2026, the discussion gradually moved beyond testing.

We started talking about how product, development, and QA teams work together. We discussed why requirements so often fall out of sync, and how AI might change the way engineering teams are organized.

By the end of the discussion, the session had become the final push that helped set our company's organizational transformation in motion.

Looking back, I find that quite interesting. We set out to help testers work more efficiently with AI. Instead, we ended up discussing how AI might force the entire engineering organization to rethink the way it works.

1. 🤖 I Wanted AI to Handle the Entire Testing Process

I've been working on a multi-agent automated testing system.

Rather than simply asking AI to generate automation scripts from test cases, I wanted to connect the entire process: understanding requirements, designing tests, executing them, reporting defects, verifying fixes, and running regression tests.

The workflow looks roughly like this:

  1. AI reads product requirement documents and prototypes to understand business workflows and acceptance criteria.
  2. It generates test cases, which are then reviewed by multiple agents.
  3. Based on those test cases, AI controls web browsers and mobile apps, simulating real user interactions to execute the tests.
  4. When it finds an issue, AI generates a defect report and submits it to our issue-tracking system.
  5. Each reported defect goes through a second review and human confirmation before being assigned to the appropriate developer.
  6. After the developer fixes the issue, AI automatically runs regression tests to verify the fix and move the defect through the closure process, with human oversight retained.

The end-to-end workflow, from requirements to regression testing, is now in place and working.

What impressed me most was that AI had started taking over some of the most frustrating parts of traditional test automation.

With UI automation, the hardest part was often not writing the initial scripts. It was maintaining them.

A developer changes a UI component, and testers may have to revisit element locators, page objects, and interaction scripts. The more frequently the interface changes, the higher the maintenance cost. Sometimes, testers spend more time maintaining automation scripts than actually running tests.

Now, AI can observe the current page, understand its elements and interaction states, and perform actions based on the testing objectives. It still has to deal with UI changes and execution failures, but it can already take over a considerable amount of work that previously required repeated manual maintenance.

That made me reconsider the limits of automated testing.

2. 🔍 Automated Testing Should Do More Than Repeat Known Test Cases


For a long time, I held a fairly firm view of automated testing:

Automation is useful for regression testing, but it is not very good at discovering new defects.

The reason is straightforward. Traditional automated testing relies heavily on test cases designed in advance, fixed execution steps, and predefined assertions. It can repeatedly execute known test paths, but it struggles to discover problems that testers never thought to look for.

It behaves more like an executor that follows instructions than a tester capable of exploring software behavior.

But as AI agents emerged that could understand requirements, observe screens, analyze page states, and adapt their actions, I began to change my mind.

When training and refining the agents' testing behavior, I emphasized one principle:

Don't just follow the requirements document. And don't treat the test cases as the limits of your exploration.

Requirements describe what a product is expected to do, but they cannot cover every possible user behavior or system state.

So, after completing the tests defined by the requirements, AI should also explore additional scenarios, including:

  • Invalid and unexpected inputs: Empty values, excessively long text, illegal characters, unusual formats, and unexpected combinations of data.
  • Boundary conditions: Maximum and minimum values, threshold conditions, duplicate submissions, and unusual sequences of operations.
  • Abnormal workflows: Interrupted operations, repeated clicks, page refreshes, network failures, expired sessions, and inconsistent states between consecutive steps.
  • Security-related scenarios: Unauthorized access, permission boundaries, sensitive information exposure, and attempts to perform operations that should not be allowed.
  • Unexpected interactions: Skipping normal steps, performing rapid consecutive actions, repeatedly switching states, or accessing the same business function through different entry points.

Of course, this does not mean AI should be allowed to operate freely against production systems. The scope of exploration, test environments, account permissions, and operational risks must all be controlled. Security testing must also remain within clearly authorized boundaries.

I don't want AI to simply prove that the requirements have been implemented. I want it to look for problems that might emerge when the system is used in ways that were never anticipated.

This is where my understanding of automated testing has changed.

In the past, automation mainly repeated checks for known issues. Now, AI has the potential to help discover problems we didn't know to look for.

It cannot guarantee that every defect will be found, and it cannot replace human judgment. But automated testing no longer has to be limited to test cases written in advance.

3. 🌙 AI Works at Night. Humans Make the Decisions During the Day.


These days, I usually schedule automated testing tasks before finishing work.

The agents then continue running overnight. When I arrive at work the next morning, I can usually find a batch of defect reports already submitted by AI.

My job is to review those issues one by one, determine whether they are genuine and consistent with the current requirements, confirm them, and assign them to the appropriate developers.

This changes how testers spend their time.

Previously, testers had to spend a considerable amount of time operating systems, executing test cases, observing results, and preparing reports. Now, AI can take over a significant portion of that repetitive work, allowing people to focus more on evaluating issues, analyzing risks, and improving product quality.

However, this process also revealed another problem:

Finding a defect doesn't mean communicating it effectively.

Initially, AI-generated defect reports were often just dense blocks of text. They contained plenty of information, but they weren't particularly easy for developers to read.

If a report cannot help the person receiving it quickly understand the problem, then even a large amount of information does little to improve collaboration.

So I went through several rounds of adjustments to the reporting format. We needed more than a record of everything that happened during execution. The report had to clearly explain what happened, where the problem occurred, how the actual behavior differed from the expected behavior, and how the issue could be reproduced and verified.

After several iterations, the reports became much more readable and useful.

This made me realize that AI output quality should not be measured only by how much work it completes. We also need to consider whether the next person in the workflow can actually use the results.

After each testing cycle, I also ask AI to summarize the problems and lessons from that run. Experiences that have been reviewed, validated, and shown to be reusable are then distilled into general-purpose Skills.

That way, the next testing cycle doesn't have to start from scratch. It can build on what the previous cycle has learned.

In practice, this creates a continuous improvement loop:

Execute → Discover issues → Review → Capture lessons → Turn reusable knowledge into Skills → Start the next cycle.

4. 📊 The Numbers Show the Value, but Also Reveal Problems


In one of our knowledge-base projects, we've accumulated some concrete results:

Metric Result
Total defects identified 47
Defects identified by AI 36
Defects identified manually 11
Defects ultimately confirmed as valid 30
Valid defects contributed by AI 21

In other words, AI identified 21 of the 30 defects ultimately confirmed as valid, accounting for 70%.

These figures show that, within the scope of this project and its test coverage, AI is no longer just a tool for executing test cases. It is making a real contribution to defect discovery.

We've also experimented with having agents navigate pages, capture the API calls involved in business workflows, and run scheduled, full-scale API validation every day. Our current test environment covers nearly 300 APIs associated with business workflows.

These experiments show that AI can take on continuous testing tasks at both the UI and API levels.

But the data also reveals some problems.

For example, we currently have only one test environment. When multiple requirements are being developed in parallel, code changes can conflict, and deployments can interrupt other testing tasks. We still need to evaluate adding a second test environment and a dedicated performance testing environment.

Browser compatibility also needs further work, including test coverage for different Windows versions and the 360 browser.

These are infrastructure problems. They can be addressed gradually through additional resources and technical improvements.

What really made me think, however, was another category of problems.

5. 🧩 Automation Exposes Organizational Problems That Traditional Testing Often Hides


At one point, we noticed that some defects reported by AI were being classified as invalid.

Our first suspicion was naturally that AI might have misunderstood the requirements or that there was a problem with the testing logic.

But after looking more closely, we found that AI wasn't entirely to blame.

Some requirements had already been adjusted through discussions between product and development, but the official PRD had not been updated. Product and development might have reached a new understanding, or even made changes to the implementation privately, while QA and AI were still working from the original requirements document.

As a result, AI identified a discrepancy based on the official requirements, but the reported issue was considered invalid.

From a testing perspective, AI hadn't necessarily done anything wrong. From the development team's perspective, based on their current understanding of the implementation, the issue might not have been something they believed needed fixing.

The real problem was that the team was working with multiple versions of the same requirement context.

This led me to an important observation:

Automation can expose organizational problems that traditional manual testing has quietly absorbed and hidden for years.

In the past, testers often compensated for inconsistencies in requirements documents through verbal communication, ad hoc clarification, and their own experience. This work is important, but it can also make an organization believe that its processes are working perfectly well.

AI doesn't automatically know about a private conversation, nor can it understand the latest version of someone's thinking. It executes tasks based on the context it receives.

When the official documentation no longer matches the team's actual understanding, automation exposes that gap.

So the question isn't simply whether AI is smart enough.

We also need to ask: Does the team have a shared version of the requirements that everyone agrees on, that is kept up to date, and that AI can correctly interpret?

6. 🏢 Why Did a Technical Presentation Turn into a Discussion About Organizational Structure?


On November 5, 2026, we held an internal session to share our experience with local AI agents and automated testing. One of the company's founders also joined the discussion.

The original focus was AI testing capabilities, but the conversation gradually expanded to engineering workflows and organizational structure.

I increasingly agree with one observation:

AI is reducing the cost of producing code, but the cost of coordinating people isn't decreasing at the same pace.

In the past, a requirement might be analyzed and documented by a product manager, handed over to frontend and backend developers, and eventually passed to QA for verification. Every handoff meant that context had to be transferred again.

If any part of that chain involved a misunderstanding, rework could follow.

Now, AI can help product managers make certain code changes. It can help testers understand and modify code. It can also allow developers to participate more directly in requirement analysis and product design.

If a small requirement only needs a few code changes, but still has to pass through multiple roles, processes, and rounds of communication, the coordination cost may far exceed the actual coding cost.

This doesn't mean professional specialization has lost its value. Rather, AI is gradually lowering some of the capability barriers between traditional roles.

During our discussion, we proposed a direction: moving away from traditional role-based division of labor toward a more flexible model in which people can work across traditional role boundaries with the help of AI.

When we talk about a full-stack approach across the team, we don't mean that everyone must become a traditional full-stack engineer, or that people should abandon their professional expertise.

What we really mean is this:

People in product, development, and QA should all be able to use AI to cross their previous technical boundaries and help solve the problems they understand.

For example:

  • Product managers can use AI to make code changes and verify smaller requirements themselves.
  • Developers can participate in requirement analysis earlier and take overall ownership of larger initiatives.
  • Testers don't have to stop at submitting bug reports when they discover defects. They can use AI to investigate the issue and even modify code, with developers providing the necessary review and confirmation.

For small requirements, we want to reduce unnecessary handoffs. For larger initiatives, we want to assign a clear owner to coordinate the entire process.

This isn't about eliminating professional roles. It's about reducing the information loss caused by rigid boundaries between them.

7. 🔗 Collaboration Should Start with Requirements, Not After Testing Finds a Problem


To make this way of working possible, we first need to address the problem of shared requirement context.

We discussed several concrete directions.

First, product, development, and QA should participate in requirement alignment from the beginning, rather than waiting until the PRD is finished and development is complete before testers start trying to understand the requirements.

Second, we want to establish a standardized PRD Skill and structured templates so that requirement documents follow a more consistent format.

More importantly, whenever requirements change, the official documentation must be updated promptly. Changes should not exist only in private conversations between a few people.

We also discussed a more ambitious idea: using recordings from smart badges to identify requirement changes during discussions, flag content that might affect the requirements, and assist in updating the PRD. The proposed changes would then be submitted to the relevant people for review and approval.

This is still an idea to be explored, not a feature that has already been deployed.

But the underlying principle is clear:

We should make sure the team's actual shared understanding is captured promptly in a form that everyone can use.

Beyond PRDs, we also need shared development and testing Skills, coding standards, and Specs.

When product, development, and QA work from a reasonably consistent context, AI can become a tool that connects different parts of the workflow instead of creating more isolated information silos between roles.

8. 🚀 From Individual AI Tools to an AI-Driven Engineering System


The discussion eventually moved beyond any particular agent or automated testing tool.

We started looking at the engineering system as a whole.

For example:

  • Building shared Skill libraries for development and testing.
  • Standardizing coding conventions and Spec management.
  • Creating a complete workflow: retrieving defects from Yunxiao, using AI to fix them, running automated regression tests, and retaining human review.
  • Exploring automated effort estimation and requirement classification.
  • Continuing to improve test environments and browser compatibility.
  • Ensuring that requirement changes are communicated promptly to reduce unnecessary discussions and rework.

These initiatives won't be completed automatically after a single meeting. The organizational transformation plan has already been launched, and progress will be reviewed and coordinated through weekly updates.

Of course, having a clear direction and an initiated plan doesn't mean the road ahead will be smooth.

Once implementation begins, we'll inevitably encounter practical obstacles: the inertia of existing processes, established collaboration habits between different roles, limitations in technical infrastructure, and the challenges of fitting new ways of working into existing business rhythms.

These problems can't be solved through one meeting or a few new rules. We'll need to identify issues as they arise, adjust our approach, and gradually develop a working model that actually fits the team.

For me, this is what makes the discussion meaningful. It wasn't just about proposing an idea for organizational change. The plan has already moved into the implementation stage.

An AI-driven engineering system can't be built simply by purchasing a few tools, connecting some APIs, or creating a handful of agents.

It requires technical capabilities, process standards, accumulated knowledge, and organizational collaboration to evolve together.

If information within the team remains inconsistent, even the most capable AI will simply execute the wrong context more efficiently.

9. 💡 In the AI Era, Coding Ability May No Longer Be the Rarest Resource


Looking back, I initially just wanted AI to help me automate more testing work.

But as AI began to understand requirements, interact with interfaces, actively explore abnormal scenarios, submit defects, assist with fixes, and perform regression testing, I realized that I needed to rethink more than just testing. I needed to rethink the entire software development process.

In the past, many efficiency problems were attributed to a lack of capability in a particular role, or to a specific stage of the process not being fast enough.

Now, AI is making more and more tasks easier.

But as writing code becomes easier, what may actually slow down development is the failure to synchronize requirements, unclear ownership, and too many handoffs between people.

I don't believe AI will turn everyone into a programmer, nor do I think software teams will no longer need professional roles such as product, development, and QA.

I believe AI will gradually remove unnecessary barriers between these roles.

People who understand a problem should be able to use AI to move toward a solution more directly, rather than having to wait for information to pass through multiple roles.

For testers, this means going beyond executing test cases to participating in risk exploration, problem analysis, and quality improvement.

For developers, it means taking responsibility not just for receiving requirements and writing code, but for solving a more complete problem.

For product managers, it means going beyond describing requirements and using AI to validate and implement their ideas more directly.

Ultimately, a team's competitiveness may no longer depend on how many people complete how many separate tasks. It may depend on whether the team can move accurate information quickly and enable everyone to use AI to solve more complete problems.

An AI testing presentation eventually became a discussion about how the entire engineering organization should change.

Perhaps this is one of the most important changes to pay attention to in the AI era:

AI is making coding easier, but what will truly make software development faster may be our willingness to redesign the way people work together.

articles.title: Trocar de provedor não deveria ser uma dor de cabeça
articles.description: Se você já trabalhou ou trabalha em startups, em um fluxo rápido de desenvolvimento de produto ou até...
articles.body_html:
Se você já trabalhou ou trabalha em startups, em um fluxo rápido de desenvolvimento de produto ou até mesmo criando o seu produto, deve saber que um produto pode e vai mudar em algum momento, devido à necessidade de novos investidores ou clientes, ou à decisão de algum stakeholder. Caso você não tenha experiência ou esteja começando agora nesse mundo de entregas rápidas, neste artigo eu pretendo te passar uma breve dica que provavelmente vai te economizar tempo de trabalho e reduzir as suas chances de ter dor de cabeça.

Sumário

  • Por que trocar de provedor
  • O provedor dentro do domínio
    • A modelagem acoplada
    • O código acoplado
  • E se o provedor mudar?
  • A solução
    • O domínio fala a própria língua
    • Um tradutor para cada provedor
    • Juntando tudo

Por que trocar de provedor

Acredito que o cenário mais comum e prático que eu possa dar para ilustrar o que eu quero te mostrar seja o caso em que você precise lidar com a mudança de um provedor de pagamento. Muitas coisas podem fazer com que uma empresa ou um produto cogite mudar o provedor, como: melhores taxas entre provedores, qualidade no suporte, maturidade do provedor e confiabilidade. Até mesmo o cenário em que o dono do provedor de pagamento é conhecido ou amigo da startup ou empresa em que você trabalha pode motivar essa mudança.

O provedor dentro do domínio

Imagine que chega a task para você fazer a implementação de um provedor de pagamento X dentro de um novo produto da empresa. Com prazo apertado e um único provedor, modelar tudo em cima dele parece o caminho mais rápido. Você faz a modelagem, faz a integração, tudo certinho: testado e funcionando. Mas aí, depois de alguns meses, chega a task para implementar um novo provedor de pagamento, e você percebe que vai ser uma dor de cabeça, porque tanto a modelagem quanto o código do domínio foram feitos com o vocabulário do antigo provedor, tornando tudo acoplado. Essa é uma situação que não é nada interessante de se resolver, mas é bem previsível de se combater.

A modelagem acoplada

O código acoplado

Aqui foi exemplificado o impacto na modelagem, mas, além dele, o código também teria outros problemas, como a repetição de código e inúmeras verificações.

final class ReleaseProduct
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        $isPaid = match ($order->provider) {
            'stripe' => $order->stripe_status === 'succeeded',
            'mercadopago' => $order->mercadopago_status === 'approved',
        };

        if (! $isPaid) {
            return;
        }

        $order->product->release();
    }
}

final class RefundOrder
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        match ($order->provider) {
            'stripe' => $this->stripe->refund($order->stripe_payment_intent_id),
            'mercadopago' => $this->mercadoPago->refund($order->mercadopago_payment_id),
        };
    }
}

E se o provedor mudar?

Eu tive o prazer de ter uma ótima liderança técnica e experiente que, antes mesmo de me deixar colocar a mão na modelagem, me mostrou as seguintes questões: "E se o provedor mudar, o que fazer? Qual a consequência de mudar do provedor X para o Y?" Sinceramente, no começo eu não fazia ideia do que fazer. Foi aí que me foi apresentada a ideia de fazer uma modelagem e um código agnóstico de provedor (provider-agnostic).

Na computação, um dispositivo ou programa de software é considerado agnóstico ou agnóstico de dados se o método ou formato de transmissão de dados for irrelevante para a função do dispositivo ou programa. Isso significa que o dispositivo ou programa pode receber dados em múltiplos formatos ou de múltiplas fontes e ainda assim processá-los de forma eficaz. — Wikipédia, tradução livre

Uma maneira prática de absorver essa ideia, e que me ajudou bastante, foi pensar: caso determinada informação possa ter um caminho diferente, tanto a modelagem quanto o código devem se comportar da mesma maneira, independentemente do caminho. No nosso exemplo, a informação é "o pagamento foi concluído", e os caminhos são o Stripe e o Mercado Pago.

Pagamento é só o exemplo que escolhi, mas a mesma ideia aparece em vários outros lugares: provedor de autenticação (Auth0, Cognito, Firebase Auth), envio de e-mail (SES, SendGrid, Mailgun), armazenamento de arquivos (S3, Google Cloud Storage) e envio de SMS (Twilio, Zenvia). Se você usa Laravel, já usa isso no dia a dia: o Mail e o Storage funcionam do mesmo jeito, seja qual for o driver configurado por trás.

A solução

O domínio fala a própria língua

Para tornar o código e a modelagem agnósticos de provedor, você vai precisar entender o que é domínio. Talvez você já tenha ouvido falar sobre DDD; é dele que vem esse termo. Não vou entrar no tema por completo (recomendo que você leia sobre o assunto depois), mas vou explicar brevemente o que seria esse tal domínio.

Entenda o domínio como a área de conhecimento e as regras do problema que o seu produto resolve. No código, ele vira a parte central, que reúne essas regras e entende como resolver o problema. No exemplo que estou utilizando, a nossa área de conhecimento e as regras são de pedido, então o nosso domínio tem tudo o que é necessário para resolver isso.

Agora que sabemos disso, você já deve ter notado que cada provedor tem uma nomenclatura para as informações de que ele precisa ou que retorna. Um pagamento concluído, por exemplo, é succeeded no Stripe e approved no Mercado Pago. Já o nosso domínio usa os próprios nomes, paid ou canceled, escolhidos por você ou pelo seu time, e os nomes dos provedores nunca chegam até ele.

Olhando para a modelagem: a tabela orders guarda só o vocabulário do domínio. O provedor vira apenas um dado (provider), e o id dele fica em uma coluna genérica (provider_reference).

Schema::create('orders', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->integer('amount_cents');
    $table->string('status');
    $table->string('provider');
    $table->string('provider_reference')->nullable();
    $table->timestamps();
});

enum PaymentStatus: string
{
    case Pending = 'pending';
    case Paid = 'paid';
    case Canceled = 'canceled';
}

enum PaymentProvider: string
{
    case Stripe = 'stripe';
    case MercadoPago = 'mercadopago';
}

final class Order extends Model
{
    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return [
            'status' => PaymentStatus::class,
            'provider' => PaymentProvider::class,
        ];
    }
}

Um tradutor para cada provedor

O próximo passo é lidar com essa diferença de nomenclatura entre os provedores. Para isso, vamos criar uma classe que faz a tradução da nomenclatura da API para o que temos no nosso domínio. Esse tradutor é um adaptador (adapter), e todos os adaptadores seguem o mesmo contrato, a porta (port) que o domínio define. Essa camada de tradução, como um todo, é o que o DDD chama de camada anticorrupção (Anti-Corruption Layer).

                   DOMÍNIO  (fala "paid", "canceled")
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReleaseProduct      RefundOrder      HandleWebhook │
  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                             │ depende só do contrato
                 ┌───────────▼────────────┐
                 │ PaymentGatewayContract │  ← porta
                 └───────────┬────────────┘
             ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
  ┌──────────▼───────────┐       ┌────────────▼───────────┐
  │ StripeGateway        │       │ MercadoPagoGateway     │  ← adaptadores
  │ "succeeded" → paid   │       │ "approved"  → paid     │    (traduzem)
  └──────────┬───────────┘       └────────────┬───────────┘
             ▼                                ▼
         API Stripe                   API Mercado Pago

Depois vem a porta, o contrato que todo provedor precisa seguir:

interface PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function charge(Order $order): string;

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus;

    public function refund(string $reference): void;
}

E um adaptador para cada provedor. É aqui, e só aqui, que o vocabulário de cada um aparece:

final class StripeGateway implements PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function __construct(private StripeApi $api) {}

    public function charge(Order $order): string
    {
        return $this->api->createPaymentIntent($order->amount_cents)->id;
    }

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus
    {
        return match ($this->api->getPaymentIntent($reference)->status) {
            'succeeded' => PaymentStatus::Paid,
            'canceled' => PaymentStatus::Canceled,
            default => PaymentStatus::Pending,
        };
    }

    public function refund(string $reference): void
    {
        $this->api->refundPaymentIntent($reference);
    }
}

final class MercadoPagoGateway implements PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function __construct(private MercadoPagoApi $api) {}

    public function charge(Order $order): string
    {
        return $this->api->createPixPayment($order->amount_cents)->id;
    }

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus
    {
        return match ($this->api->getPayment($reference)->status) {
            'approved' => PaymentStatus::Paid,
            'cancelled', 'rejected' => PaymentStatus::Canceled,
            default => PaymentStatus::Pending,
        };
    }

    public function refund(string $reference): void
    {
        $this->api->refundPayment($reference);
    }
}

Juntando tudo

A configuração diz qual provedor está ativo:

// config/payments.php
return [
    'default' => env('PAYMENT_PROVIDER', 'stripe'),
];

Um resolver sabe qual adaptador corresponde a cada provedor:

final class PaymentGatewayResolver
{
    public function for(PaymentProvider $provider): PaymentGatewayContract
    {
        return match ($provider) {
            PaymentProvider::Stripe => app(StripeGateway::class),
            PaymentProvider::MercadoPago => app(MercadoPagoGateway::class),
        };
    }
}

E o container do Laravel junta os dois: entrega o adaptador do provedor ativo para qualquer classe que peça o contrato.

final class AppServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider
{
    public function register(): void
    {
        $this->app->bind(
            PaymentGatewayContract::class,
            fn () => app(PaymentGatewayResolver::class)
                ->for(PaymentProvider::from(config('payments.default'))),
        );
    }
}

Com isso, aquelas classes do começo do artigo deixam de saber qual provedor está por trás:

final class ReleaseProduct
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        if ($order->status !== PaymentStatus::Paid) {
            return;
        }

        $order->product->release();
    }
}

final class RefundOrder
{
    public function __construct(private PaymentGatewayContract $gateway) {}

    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        $this->gateway->refund($order->provider_reference);
    }
}

Se amanhã chegar a task de um terceiro provedor, o trabalho é criar um adaptador novo, adicionar um caso no enum PaymentProvider e uma linha no PaymentGatewayResolver. A tabela orders, o ReleaseProduct e o RefundOrder continuam iguais.

articles.title: When an AI Agent Says 'Done,' What Exactly Has Finished?
articles.description: "Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session.  It can also conceal three...
articles.body_html:
"Done." It's probably the most satisfying word in a coding-agent session.

It can also conceal three very different questions:

  1. Was the work permitted?
  2. Did the work actually happen?
  3. Did the result achieve what we needed?

All three matter. A single green checkmark can make them look like one decision.

A small scenario

Imagine asking a coding agent to update validation logic under src/**.

It edits the code, reports that its tests passed, and declares the task complete. Everything looks fine until you ask what the status actually proves.

  • The task was assigned to an implementer with a declared src/** write scope. But did the runtime enforce that scope for the tools the agent used?
  • The plan called for independent review. But who actually reviewed the final revision, and was that the revision ultimately merged?
  • The agent says the feature works. But was that checked in the environment where users experience it?

These are separate evidence problems. Passing a test suite answers something useful about the tested code. It cannot, by itself, answer the other two questions.

One failure you can reproduce without an AI model

I maintain Agent Role Contracts (ARC), an open-source checker for declared agent roles, scope, reviews, and handoffs.

Its quickstart uses a deliberately simple setup:

Declared rule Requested task Preflight result
Implementer may write within src/** Update src/example.mjs PASS
Same declared rule Update secrets/production.txt TASK_WRITE_SCOPE_OUTSIDE_AUTHORITY
Same declared rule Correct the request to src/example.mjs PASS

You can run the published source demo with Git, Node.js 22.5+, and npm:

git clone https://github.com/suirindo/agent-role-contracts.git
npm --prefix agent-role-contracts run demo --silent

The repository's documented sequence is PASS → expected FAIL → PASS. It reads fictional JSON declarations; it starts no agent and writes no target file. The intentional rejection demonstrates one narrow property: a requested scope conflicts with the declared authority.

That's useful precisely because the check has a clear boundary. A declaration PASS does not authenticate the executor, enforce filesystem permissions, verify an actual review, or authorize execution. The host system must supply those controls.

A completion report with three layers

For real work, I'd like completion reports to distinguish these layers:

Layer A useful receipt What remains to establish
Contract Current task, scope, responsible role, review route, and the check result Whether the declared actors and permissions are genuine
Execution Exact commit or artifact, command results, and observable side-effect receipts Whether anything unobserved or uncertain occurred
Acceptance Independent review of the exact candidate, acceptance tests, and production observation where relevant Whether the user-facing outcome meets the original request

That produces a much more useful sentence than "Done":

Implementation completed and local tests passed. Independent review is pending. Production behavior has not yet been checked.

It is less triumphant. It is much more actionable.

The uncomfortable question

As agents become more autonomous, the word complete is becoming a product-interface decision. If the interface compresses implementation, verification, and acceptance into one status, the human operator inherits the uncertainty later.

Some teams will reasonably keep these stages separate in CI, IAM, and their runtime. Others may want a small declaration check before dispatch. ARC handles that narrower declaration problem; the broader evidence chain belongs to the surrounding system.

For teams using coding agents today: what is the minimum evidence you require before an agent is allowed to say "done"?

Is a passing test suite enough for internal tasks? Do you require an independent reviewer, an exact artifact identifier, a live check, or different thresholds depending on the side effect?

I'd be particularly interested in answers from teams that have already found a simpler solution.

Disclosure: I maintain Agent Role Contracts at Netsujo. The example above is a synthetic declaration check, not a production incident. Read the quickstart and limitations.

articles.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
articles.description: DateTime.Now is DateTime.UtcNow plus a trip through your local time zone rules, and that trip isn't free in a hot loop. I counted: on a box with a real time zone it roughly doubles the cost of reading the clock.
articles.body_html:
I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock.

So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted.

Now is UtcNow wearing a coat

DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all.

The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero.

Putting a clock on the clock

I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. Same loop, three bodies.

static long ReadUtcNow() => DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks;
static long ReadNow()    => DateTime.Now.Ticks;
static long ReadStopwatch() => Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

First run, on the container as it ships, which pins itself to UTC:

Local time zone: Etc/UTC

20,000,000 reads, best of 5
  DateTime.UtcNow     661.5 ms     33.1 ns/call
  DateTime.Now        911.8 ms     45.6 ns/call
  Now / UtcNow         1.38x

A UTC box has a zero offset. There's nothing to add. And Now is still almost 40% slower, because it does the lookup to find out the offset is zero. The work happens whether or not it changes the answer.

Then I pointed TZ at a real zone, the kind your laptop or an on-prem server actually runs, with daylight saving rules to evaluate:

Local time zone: America/New_York

20,000,000 reads, best of 5
  DateTime.UtcNow     678.3 ms     33.9 ns/call
  DateTime.Now      1,357.2 ms     67.9 ns/call
  Now / UtcNow         2.00x

Twice the cost. UtcNow sits around 33 ns no matter what I do; Now lands somewhere between 60 and 68 ns across runs. The time zone isn't part of reading the clock. It's a question Now asks afterward, every single time.

This is a container, not a lab, so I care about the ratio, not the exact nanoseconds. The ratio was steady run to run. Roughly double on a real zone, roughly a third extra on UTC.

The tool I actually wanted

Half the time I reach for DateTime.Now I'm not even recording a wall-clock time. I'm measuring how long something took. For that, both Now and UtcNow are the wrong tool, because they drag calendar math into a job that's really just "count ticks between here and there." Stopwatch does exactly that and nothing else:

  Stopwatch.GetTimestamp   637.3 ms     31.9 ns/call

Cheapest of the three, and it never touches a time zone or even cares what day it is. If you're timing a block of code, this is the one.

When I'd leave it alone

If you call DateTime.Now a handful of times per request, this whole post is noise. Thirty-odd extra nanoseconds disappears against literally anything else your code does. I'm not going to rewrite a login handler to shave that off, and neither should you. The importer only cared because it was reading the clock once per row, hundreds of thousands of times, in a loop that otherwise did very little. Hot path, high count. That's the only place it shows up.

And don't go blindly swapping Now for UtcNow in display code. If you're formatting a timestamp a human is going to read, they want their local time, and UtcNow will happily show them the wrong hour. That's a correctness bug, and no benchmark makes it worth shipping.

My own rule, for what it's worth: compute and store in UTC, read the clock with UtcNow, time things with Stopwatch, and convert to local exactly once, at the edge, right before a person sees it. Local time is a presentation concern. Treating it like a data concern is how you end up paying the time zone tax a few hundred thousand times to import a file nobody's even looking at yet.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. New console project targeting net10.0, drop this in Program.cs, then dotnet run -c Release, and TZ="America/New_York" dotnet run -c Release for the wider gap:

using System.Diagnostics;

Console.WriteLine($"Local time zone: {TimeZoneInfo.Local.Id}");

const int Iterations = 20_000_000;
const int Rounds = 5;

// Warm up both paths so the JIT and the time-zone cache are hot.
_ = Measure(ReadUtcNow, 1_000_000);
_ = Measure(ReadNow, 1_000_000);

long utcTicks = long.MaxValue, nowTicks = long.MaxValue, swTicks = long.MaxValue;
for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
{
    utcTicks = Math.Min(utcTicks, Measure(ReadUtcNow, Iterations));
    nowTicks = Math.Min(nowTicks, Measure(ReadNow, Iterations));
    swTicks  = Math.Min(swTicks,  Measure(ReadStopwatch, Iterations));
}

double utcMs = utcTicks * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;
double nowMs = nowTicks * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;
double swMs  = swTicks  * 1000.0 / Stopwatch.Frequency;

Console.WriteLine($"{Iterations:N0} reads, best of {Rounds}");
Console.WriteLine($"  DateTime.UtcNow        {utcMs,8:N1} ms   {utcMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");
Console.WriteLine($"  DateTime.Now           {nowMs,8:N1} ms   {nowMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");
Console.WriteLine($"  Now / UtcNow           {nowMs / utcMs,8:N2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"  Stopwatch.GetTimestamp {swMs,8:N1} ms   {swMs * 1e6 / Iterations,5:N1} ns/call");

return;

static long Measure(Func<long> body, int iterations)
{
    long sink = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++)
        sink += body();
    sw.Stop();
    if (sink == -1) Console.WriteLine("unreachable"); // keep the loop alive
    return sw.ElapsedTicks;
}

static long ReadUtcNow() => DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks;
static long ReadNow() => DateTime.Now.Ticks;
static long ReadStopwatch() => Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();

Do you default to Now or UtcNow when you're not thinking about it? I'd bet most of us type whichever one our fingers learned first. Curious which camp you're in.

— still putting clocks on things nobody asked me to time

articles.title: I Expected a 100x JSON Slowdown. I Got 1.9x.
articles.description: I benchmarked the old 'never build a new JsonSerializerOptions per call' rule on .NET 10, expecting the famous 100x penalty. I got 1.9x. Here's why the runtime now rescues you, and the one case where it still doesn't.
articles.body_html:
I had a little serialize helper that sailed through code review. It looked like this: return JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { ... }). A fresh options object, built right there in the method, on every call. Every post I'd ever half-read told me this was a cardinal sin, the kind that turns a fast endpoint slow and earns you a 100x regression. So I braced for the worst, wrote a benchmark, and went hunting for the catastrophe.

I didn't find it. On the path my code actually took, I got 1.9x. That was surprising enough that I kept pulling the thread, and the real answer turned out to be more useful than the scary one.

The three ways to get options wrong (and right)

Here's the payload. A small order, the kind of thing a handler serializes thousands of times a second.

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, DateTime PlacedAtUtc, LineItem[] Items, string? Note);
record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);

And here are the three ways I serialized it. Case A is the fix everyone recommends: build the options once, reuse the instance.

// A — one shared instance, reused everywhere.
var shared = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
};
string SerializeShared(Order o) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, shared);

Case B is my sin: a new instance every call, but with the exact same configuration each time. This is what the accidental version almost always looks like in real code.

// B — new instance each call, identical config.
static string SerializeNewSameConfig(Order o)
{
    var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
    {
        PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
        DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
    };
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, options);
}

Case C is the one I didn't write but easily could have: a new instance each call where the configuration also changes. Here I just nudge MaxDepth to make every instance distinct, but in the wild this is what you get when options are assembled from per-request data.

// C — new instance each call, config varies.
static string SerializeNewVaryingConfig(Order o, int i)
{
    var options = new JsonSerializerOptions
    {
        PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
        DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
        MaxDepth = 32 + (i & 63) // harmless, but makes every instance distinct
    };
    return JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, options);
}

The measurement is boring on purpose: warm up a thousand times so the JIT and first-use caches aren't in the number, collect garbage, then time 200,000 serializations and take the best of five rounds. I also grab GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around the loop so I can see the allocations, not just the clock.

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(Func<Order, string> fn, Order o, int iterations)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) _ = fn(o);
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();

    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) _ = fn(o);
    sw.Stop();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
}

What came out

This isn't a lab. It's a 2-core container on .NET 10, best-of-five, and I care about the ratios, not the absolute milliseconds.

Iterations per run: 200,000

A shared instance        :     153.7 ms      186.2 MB
B new, same config       :     295.6 ms      224.7 MB
C new, varying config    :     593.9 ms      329.5 MB

B vs A :    1.9x time     1.2x alloc
C vs A :    3.9x time     1.8x alloc

So my supposedly-criminal Case B costs about 1.9x the time and 1.2x the memory. Real, worth fixing, but nowhere near the horror story.

Why B isn't the disaster the internet promised

The reason is something JsonSerializerOptions does behind your back. The expensive part of serialization isn't the writing. It's building the metadata that describes how to walk your type (JsonTypeInfo for Order, LineItem, and every property). Years ago, each options instance built and cached that metadata on itself, so a new instance per call meant rebuilding the whole thing every single time. That's where the 100x stories came from.

Modern .NET keeps a cache keyed on the options configuration, not just the instance. When I create a new options object with the same settings as one it's already seen, the runtime recognizes the configuration and reuses the metadata it built before. I still pay to allocate the object and do the equivalence lookup every call, which is the 1.9x, but I don't pay to rebuild the metadata, the part that used to hurt.

Case C is where that safety net has a hole. Every instance there has a different MaxDepth, so the configuration never matches and the cache can't help. Close to 4x and climbing. The lesson isn't that new is fine now. The penalty scales with how different your options are, and a per-call object is one small refactor away from becoming the per-request-varying kind.

What I actually do

I still make it static readonly and reuse it. Not because 1.9x scares me. On a background job that serializes once an hour I genuinely would not care, and you shouldn't either. I do it because a new JsonSerializerOptions sitting inside a hot method is a smell. It's the thing that looks innocent until someone adds options.Converters.Add(somethingFromTheRequest) six months later and tips you into Case C. Reusing one instance closes that door before anyone can walk through it.

If you want to confirm the shape on your own hardware, here's the full runnable program, a net10.0 console project. Drop it in Program.cs and dotnet run -c Release. (My usual repo push got blocked by a sandbox permission hiccup this run, so you get the whole thing right here instead of a link.)

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Text.Json;
using System.Text.Json.Serialization;

var order = new Order(
    Guid.Parse("8a1f6c2e-0b3d-4e5a-9c7f-112233445566"),
    "Acme Robotics",
    new DateTime(2026, 11, 6, 7, 10, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc),
    [ new("Servo motor", 4, 23.50m), new("Control board", 1, 189.00m), new("Cable harness", 2, 7.25m) ],
    "Leave at the loading dock");

const int Iterations = 200_000;

var shared = new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
};
string A(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, shared);

static string B(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull
});

static string C(Order o, int i) => JsonSerializer.Serialize(o, new JsonSerializerOptions
{
    PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase,
    DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull,
    MaxDepth = 32 + (i & 63)
});

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(Func<Order, int, string> fn, Order o, int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) _ = fn(o, i);
    GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); GC.Collect();
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) _ = fn(o, i);
    sw.Stop();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() - before);
}

static (double ms, long bytes) BestOf(Func<Order, int, string> fn, Order o, int n, int rounds)
{
    double best = double.MaxValue; long bytes = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++)
    {
        var (ms, b) = Measure(fn, o, n);
        if (ms < best) { best = ms; bytes = b; }
    }
    return (best, bytes);
}

var a = BestOf(A, order, Iterations, 5);
var b = BestOf(B, order, Iterations, 5);
var c = BestOf(C, order, Iterations, 5);

Console.WriteLine($"Iterations per run: {Iterations:N0}\n");
Console.WriteLine($"A shared instance        : {a.ms,9:N1} ms   {a.bytes / 1048576.0,8:N1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"B new, same config       : {b.ms,9:N1} ms   {b.bytes / 1048576.0,8:N1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"C new, varying config    : {c.ms,9:N1} ms   {c.bytes / 1048576.0,8:N1} MB\n");
Console.WriteLine($"B vs A : {b.ms / a.ms,5:N1}x time   {(double)b.bytes / a.bytes,4:N1}x alloc");
Console.WriteLine($"C vs A : {c.ms / a.ms,5:N1}x time   {(double)c.bytes / a.bytes,4:N1}x alloc");

record Order(Guid Id, string Customer, DateTime PlacedAtUtc, LineItem[] Items, string? Note);
record LineItem(string Name, int Quantity, decimal UnitPrice);

Have you ever gone looking for a legendary performance bug and found it had quietly been fixed out from under you? I'd love to hear which one.

articles.title: "Receipts, Not Vibes: Why Agent Memory Needs Provenance"
articles.description: Description: Agent memory is only useful if every claim traces back to a real incident. A practical...
articles.body_html:
Description: Agent memory is only useful if every claim traces back to a real incident. A practical look at provenance, structured metadata, and retrieval that shows its receipts.
It is 02:14 and checkout is failing. A generic model looks at the alert and says something reasonable: restart the affected pods, check the deploy dashboard, watch the error rate. It is not wrong. It is also not useful. It has no idea that this exact failure happened six weeks ago, that the cause was a missing composite index, that Priya fixed it in six minutes, or that restarting only buys forty minutes.

The difference between those two answers is not model quality. It is provenance.

When an agent claims to remember, the first question an on-call engineer should ask is: show me. Show me the incident. Show me the signals that matched. Show me who fixed it and whether the fix held. Without that, "memory" is just confident improvisation with extra steps.

That constraint shaped Déjà Vu, an on-call SRE agent built on Hindsight. Every answer is assembled from retained incidents, and every claim carries a receipt back to one.

Memory is a data model problem before it is a retrieval problem

The usual approach is to store chat transcripts and hope semantic search finds something useful. That works for a demo and fails an audit. A paragraph of postmortem prose does not tell you which incident it came from, which engineer owned it, how long the fix took, or whether the fix actually held.

So each incident is retained as a structured document. The narrative is there, because meaning matters, but so is the metadata that survives retrieval: incident id, service, root cause, fix, outcome, duration, engineer, severity and tags. Hindsight's memory documentation describes this as retaining what the system should remember, not just what was said. That distinction is the whole game.

A retain payload from the project looks roughly like this:

memory.retain({
    "bank": "dejavu-oncall",
    "content": f"{title}. {symptom}\n\nROOT CAUSE: {root}\nFIX: {fix}",
    "metadata": {
        "incident_id": iid,
        "service": service,
        "root_cause": root,
        "fix": fix,
        "outcome": outcome,
        "fix_minutes": minutes,
        "engineer": engineer,
        "severity": severity,
        "source": "seed" if seeded else "live",
    },
    "tags": [service, severity, outcome],
})

Because the metadata is stored alongside the text, a recalled paragraph becomes a citation instead of a suggestion.

Retrieval is a ranking problem

Semantic similarity alone is not enough for incidents. Two alerts can read almost identically and have completely different causes. A checkout latency spike caused by a missing index looks a lot like a checkout latency spike caused by a connection leak — until you compare the signals.

Déjà Vu builds its recall query from the alert fingerprint: service, title, body, and every key=value signal. Candidates come back from Hindsight by meaning, then the application re-ranks them against the live fingerprint. Signal similarity carries the most weight, text similarity next, coverage after that. Outcome, recency and support act as tie-breakers, and stale memories are penalised rather than silently trusted.

That last part matters. A memory bank that never forgets becomes a liability. An incident from fourteen months ago, before an architecture change, should not outrank last week's lesson just because the wording is close.

The UI has to make the receipt visible

Provenance is not a backend property. If the engineer cannot see it in three seconds, it does not exist.

In Déjà Vu, every answer carries a receipt strip: incident id, date, service, the fix that worked, the engineer, the minutes, and the outcome. The answer also states which look-alike incident it ruled out and why. The memory bus at the bottom of the screen shows the actual retain and recall operations with backend, latency and result count, so the claim is observable rather than asserted.

This is also where the honest failure mode lives. If Hindsight is unreachable, the app does not pretend. It serves the same corpus through a BM25 index over the SQLite mirror, changes the header badge from HINDSIGHT to BM25 FALLBACK, and records the path in the trace. An agent that hides its retrieval path is not trustworthy at 3 a.m.

What provenance buys you

The practical result is a different kind of answer. Without memory: generic triage, roughly 31% confidence, no owner, no time estimate, nothing to audit. With memory: the missing index, the receipts, a named engineer, a six-minute fix, and a stated reason the connection-leak theory was rejected — around 97% confidence.

The second answer is not better because the model is smarter. It is better because the model was handed evidence.

That is the case for agent memory in production systems. Not a chatbot with a longer context window. A system that remembers specific incidents, cites them, learns from resolutions, and can be checked afterwards.

If you are building in this space, start with the receipt. Decide what a citation must contain, then design retention and retrieval backwards from it. The Hindsight repository is open source, and the Vectorize primer on agent memory is a good place to pressure-test the model. Memory is only valuable when someone can verify it.

The running agent is at dejavu-tau.vercel.app, and the source is at github.com/abinivesh-m/dejavu.

articles.title: Title: The Memory That Knows When It Is Wrong
articles.description: Description: Perfect recall is dangerous without discrimination. How one agent stores the signal that...
articles.body_html:
Description: Perfect recall is dangerous without discrimination. How one agent stores the signal that separates look-alike incidents, flags stale memories, and hedges instead of guessing.

Most conversations about agent memory focus on recall. Can the agent find the right thing? That is the easy half.

The harder half is knowing when the thing it found is not the right thing.

Incident response is full of look-alikes. A p99 spike is a symptom, not a cause. Connection-pool exhaustion can come from a missing database index, a connection leak in a retry wrapper, a config rollout that lowered the pool ceiling, or a retry storm multiplying requests. The dashboards look similar. The fixes are completely different. An agent with perfect recall and no discrimination is dangerous, because it will confidently apply last month's fix to this month's failure.

Déjà Vu, an on-call SRE agent built on Hindsight, treats discrimination as a first-class part of memory rather than an afterthought.

Every memory carries its own disambiguator

When an incident is retained, it does not only store the symptom and the fix. It stores the signal that distinguishes this failure class from its nearest neighbour. A missing-index incident records that pool wait was high, database CPU was moderate, and the deploy touched only the orders schema. A connection-leak incident records that connections climbed monotonically and never dropped. A config incident records that the pool size itself changed.

That field is called the discriminator, and it is retained alongside the narrative:

doc = f"""
INCIDENT {iid} | {service} | {severity}
SYMPTOM: {symptom}
SIGNALS: {signals}
ROOT CAUSE: {root}
FIX: {fix}
HOW WE TOLD IT APART: {discriminator}
OUTCOME: {outcome} in {minutes} min by {engineer}
"""

During recall, the agent does not just retrieve candidates. It re-ranks them against the live alert fingerprint, then asks a second question: does the evidence actually rule out the obvious alternative? The answer is shown to the engineer, not hidden in a chain of thought. If the agent says this is a missing index, it also says why it is not a connection leak.

This is the difference between a search result and a diagnosis.

Stale memory is worse than no memory

Memory decays. Services get rewritten. A fix that worked in August can be actively harmful in November if the schema, the runtime or the deployment pipeline changed underneath it.

A bank that only grows becomes a museum of outdated advice. So memory needs an expiry model, even a simple one. Déjà Vu flags memories for revalidation when they are old or when their outcome was not a clean resolution, and it applies a penalty during ranking rather than treating every recalled paragraph as equally authoritative. The Memory tab exposes the count directly: retained incidents, learned live, and stale.

The stale counter is not decoration. It is a promise that the agent knows the difference between we solved this once and we still believe this.

The contradiction guard

The most useful behaviour in the whole system is the contradiction pass. After the hypothesis is formed, a critic role checks it against the strongest competing memory. If the evidence for the proposed cause is weak, or if the look-alike explains the signals better, the answer changes.

On a checkout alert, the database index story is compelling: high pool wait, moderate database CPU, a deploy minutes earlier. But a connection-leak memory has almost the same surface. The discriminator settles it. The agent states which one the signals support and which one it ruled out.

That check is also why the system does not always answer with maximum confidence. A confident wrong answer is the worst possible output for an on-call engineer. A slightly hedged answer with a stated contradiction is far more useful, because it tells the human what to verify.

Graceful degradation is part of correctness

Retrieval can fail. The memory server can be down, the network can be partitioned, the bank can be empty. A system that collapses in those moments is not production software.

If Hindsight is unreachable, Déjà Vu falls back to a BM25 index over the same SQLite mirror. The answer still carries receipts from the local corpus. The header badge changes from HINDSIGHT to BM25 FALLBACK, and the trace shows which path served the answer. The quality drops, but the honesty does not.

That design choice came from a simple test: would I trust this thing during an actual incident? Only if it tells me when it is operating in a degraded mode. Silent fallback is how agents lose trust.

What this looks like in practice

The same alert, answered twice, is the clearest demonstration. Without memory, the agent produces generic triage at roughly 31% confidence: restart the pods, check the deploy dashboard, no owner, no fix time, nothing to audit. With memory and the contradiction check, it names the missing composite index, cites three incidents, identifies the engineer who fixed it in six minutes, and explains why the connection-leak theory was rejected.

The improvement is not only in the answer. It is in the shape of the answer. Verifiable, scoped, and aware of its own uncertainty.

If you are building agents that act on operational systems, treat memory as two problems: what to remember, and how to know when the memory does not apply. The first gets the demo. The second gets production trust.

The Hindsight project provides the retention and recall primitives; the Hindsight docs cover the API; and the Vectorize memory primer is a useful grounding in the underlying ideas. Build the discrimination layer yourself. It is where the product lives.

The running agent is at dejavu-tau.vercel.app, and the source is at github.com/abinivesh-m/dejavu.
