articles.description: Reproducible is not correct   Here is a measurement you can reproduce in eight lines, plus a...
articles.body_html:
Reproducible is not correct

Here is a measurement you can reproduce in eight lines, plus a dozen-line helper. It is from the example plans that ship with my floor-plan compiler — a U-shaped house built around a courtyard:

import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { describe } from "@chanmeng666/archlang";

// Ray casting: count crossings of a ray from `point` towards +x. Points on an edge count as inside.
function pointInPolygon({ x, y }, polygon) {
  let inside = false;
  for (let i = 0, j = polygon.length - 1; i < polygon.length; j = i++) {
    const a = polygon[i], b = polygon[j];
    const cross = (b.x - a.x) * (y - a.y) - (b.y - a.y) * (x - a.x);
    const onEdge = cross === 0 &&
      Math.min(a.x, b.x) <= x && x <= Math.max(a.x, b.x) &&
      Math.min(a.y, b.y) <= y && y <= Math.max(a.y, b.y);
    if (onEdge) return true;
    if ((a.y > y) !== (b.y > y) && x < a.x + ((y - a.y) * (b.x - a.x)) / (b.y - a.y)) inside = !inside;
  }
  return inside;
}

const d = describe(readFileSync("examples/courtyard-house.arch", "utf8"));

for (const r of d.rooms) {
  const c = { x: r.bbox.x + r.bbox.w / 2, y: r.bbox.y + r.bbox.h / 2 };
  console.log(r.label, r.floor_polygon.length, "pts, bbox centre inside floor?", pointInPolygon(c, r.floor_polygon));
}
// Living 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
// Entry 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
// Dining 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
// Gallery 8 pts, bbox centre inside floor? false   <-- here
// Bedroom 1 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
// …

The Gallery is an eight-point room wrapped around a courtyard. Its bounding box has a centre, that centre is a perfectly good coordinate, and it is outside the room. Anything that reached for that point — to place a label, to start a route, to decide which side of a wall is "outside" — got a confident, silent, wrong answer.

That is not one bug. It is a defect class, and my project shipped six instances of it before anybody noticed. This post is about the three classes I have actually shipped, and what each one taught me about the difference between a gate that is green and a system that is right.

Class 1: a position derived from a shape's box instead of its shape

The six instances, all fixed in one release, all silent while they lived:

  • the point a room's name and area are drawn at;
  • the anchor a circulation route starts from — one plan reported a 10.9 m walk as 5.6 m;
  • the witness lines of automatic dimensions, which floated metres off a sloped facade;
  • swing into <room>, which gave a door a swing into a wall the room does not border;
  • furniture placed against wall, which backed a piece onto a wall outside its own room;
  • and the compass direction a window faces, which on a courtyard plan was reported backwards for every window, because the code found "outward" by comparing against the midpoint of the building's bounding box, and on a courtyard plan that midpoint sits in the courtyard.

Every one of them passed the whole test suite. Every one of them produced plausible output. The linter — the part of the system whose entire job is to say when a plan is unsound — reported none of them, because a wrong label position is not an unsound building, it is a correct building described wrongly.

What actually finds this class: not a test, a grep. Search for consumers of room.size or r.size.w with no nearby branch on the room's polygon. That pattern is a shape consumer reading the box when the ring is the honest datum. The fix is local and closed-form every time — probe one wall thickness off each face and ask which side has floor — and the general rule is the one sentence I wish I had written three releases earlier: a derived position comes from the shape, never from its bounding box or centroid.

Why a rectangle hides it. On a rectangular room the box centre is inside the room, and every one of those six code paths is correct. The entire class is invisible until a room is L-shaped, U-shaped, polygonal or round. If your fixtures are all rectangles, your suite is measuring the easy half of your input space.

Class 2: a generator that reproduces the same wrong text forever

I have a CI gate that regenerates every generated artifact and fails if the committed file differs. Grammars, error-code documentation, CLI reference, JSON schemas, a one-page language spec. It is a good gate. It has been green for a very long time.

It is also, on its own, vacuous — and this is the part that took me longest to see.

The gate compares a generator's output against the committed file. That proves the artifact is reproducible. It says nothing whatsoever about whether the generator is right. A generator that hardcodes a language fact instead of deriving it will reproduce the same wrong text on every run, for every release, with a green check beside it the whole way.

Both halves of that happened here, and both are in the public changelog:

  • the spec generator shipped a CLI reference three versions out of date, and omitted a keyword entirely, for three releases;
  • the grammar generator hardcoded a number regex that did not include the unit suffixes the lexer had accepted for months. The published grammar and the actual parser disagreed about the language, and nothing could see it, because each was internally consistent.

The rule that came out of it: a generator must derive from the source of truth — the same tables the compiler itself reads — and never retype it. And each generator needs a guard that fails when a source-of-truth entry has no rendering at all, because a missing row is exactly what a reflexive gate cannot notice.

The general form is worth stating on its own, because it is not specific to compilers:

A reflexive check is sound for a derived artifact and vacuous for a retyped one, and it cannot tell you which kind it is looking at.

Class 3: a surface no test ever executed

The third class is the cheapest to describe and the most embarrassing to find.

One release found five of them at once. A watch command that had not actually watched for files since it was written, across roughly two dozen releases. A PDF export that drew none of the wall hatching the SVG export drew. A formatter that rewrote pocket doors as hinged ones — silently changing the plan it was asked to tidy.

All five were found by running the surface. None of them by reading the code, and none of them by the test suite, which exercised the functions underneath each surface perfectly well and never once invoked the surface itself.

If you have a CLI, a formatter, a watcher or an exporter that is tested only through its internals, you have this class. The test that would have caught all five is unglamorous: run the actual command, on an actual file, and assert on what comes out.

What I do differently now

Three habits, one per class:

  1. Every new language form ships with a byte-identity law, pinned by a test. A plan that does not use the new feature must render, describe and lint exactly as it did before — proved with a hash sweep across every shipped example, not by looking at two drawings. When a golden moves, that is a finding to explain before it is a diff to bless.
  2. A green gate is asked what it proves. "Reproducible" and "correct" are different words and the gate only ever said the first one. Where a check is reflexive, the second check is a human deriving the artifact from the source of truth by hand, once, and comparing.
  3. Non-rectangular fixtures exist in the suite now. The courtyard plan at the top of this post is in the repository precisely because it is the shape that exposes class 1. A test corpus made only of easy inputs is a measurement of the easy inputs.

None of this makes the system correct. It makes a specific family of silent wrong answers loud, which is a smaller claim and the only one I can support.

Reproduce it

Save the snippet at the top of this post as check.mjs, then:

mkdir bbox-check && cd bbox-check
npm init -y && npm install @chanmeng666/archlang@1.57.0
cp -r node_modules/@chanmeng666/archlang/examples .   # the example plans ship in the package
cp ../check.mjs . && node check.mjs

which prints, against version 1.57.0:

Living 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Entry 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Dining 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Gallery 8 pts, bbox centre inside floor? false
Bedroom 1 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Bedroom 2 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Bedroom 3 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Study 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Kitchen 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Bathroom 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true
Utility 4 pts, bbox centre inside floor? true

The compiler is MIT, has zero runtime dependencies, and compiles floor plans written as text to SVG, DXF and PDF: https://archlang.uk. There is a playground if you would rather not install anything: https://playground.archlang.uk.

If you have shipped one of these three, I would genuinely like to read about it. The first class in particular seems like something everyone with geometry in their system hits exactly once.

articles.title: Prisma ORM 7's Rust-free query engine speeds up queries and slows down cold starts
articles.description: I measured Prisma ORM 7.10.1's Rust-free client against the old Rust engine on SQLite: roughly 3x faster on repeated single-row lookups, roughly 3x slower from cold start to first query, and node_modules grew 31% instead of shrinking.
articles.body_html:
Prisma's own blog says its new query engine is 85-90% smaller and up to four times faster. I installed it next to the engine it replaces and measured both claims on my own machine. The speed claim held up almost exactly. The size claim did not: node_modules came out 31% bigger, not smaller.

Prisma ORM removed its Rust query engine in version 7, released in November 2025, in favour of a TypeScript/WebAssembly "query compiler" that talks to your database through a JavaScript driver adapter instead of a native binary. It's the default now on 7.10.1, which shipped on 15 October 2026, so most people upgrading from Prisma 6 this year are about to hit this change whether they asked for it or not. I wanted to know what it actually costs and saves, not what the migration guide says it costs and saves.

I built two identical projects, same two-model schema, same SQLite database, same seed data. One used prisma@6.19.3 with the classic prisma-client-js generator and its Rust engine. The other used prisma@7.10.1 with the new prisma-client generator, the @prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3 driver adapter, and a prisma.config.ts file, because the old url = "file:./dev.db" line in the datasource block is simply rejected now.

The number that matches the marketing

I ran 2,000 sequential findUnique calls against a table of 2,000 seeded users, three times each, after the connection was already warm.

Prisma 6 (Rust engine) Prisma 7.10.1 (Rust-free)
2,000 single-row lookups 1,165 / 1,170 / 1,292 ms 379 / 370 / 422 ms
Per lookup, average ~0.60 ms ~0.19 ms

That's a 3.1x speed-up, sitting right inside Prisma's own "three to four times faster" claim. I didn't expect a vendor number to hold up this cleanly, but for this specific shape of workload — a prepared single-row query run repeatedly on a warm connection — it did.

Inserts told a different story. Seeding the same 2,000 rows one at a time took 4,957-7,436 ms on the old engine and 4,181-7,093 ms on the new one, which is the same number inside measurement noise. Neither engine is the bottleneck for sequential writes to a SQLite file with default journalling; the disk and the journal mode are. Prisma's speed claims are about reads, and testing only reads would have made the post look better than the change actually is.

The number that contradicts the marketing

The 85-90% size reduction is framed around the query engine artifact itself: a 14 MB Rust binary against a 1.6 MB compiled TypeScript bundle. That comparison is real, but it isn't what lands in your project.

$ du -sb node_modules    # prisma 6 project
266428327 node_modules   # 254.1 MiB

$ du -sb node_modules    # prisma 7.10.1 project
349344415 node_modules   # 333.3 MiB

31% bigger, not 85-90% smaller. Some of that is the driver adapter and better-sqlite3's native bindings (27 MB), which Prisma 6 didn't need at all because the Rust engine spoke to SQLite directly. But most of it is that @prisma/client still ships a WebAssembly query compiler for every supported database, in two size tiers, "fast" and "small":

$ ls -la node_modules/@prisma/client/runtime/query_compiler_*sqlite*
4406183  query_compiler_fast_bg.sqlite.wasm-base64.js
2214935  query_compiler_small_bg.sqlite.wasm-base64.js

The old engine's SQLite WASM fallback was 2,895,111 bytes. The new "fast" compiler for the same database is 4.4 MB — bigger, not smaller. Only the "small" variant comes in under the old number, and only by about 24%. Multiply either one by five supported databases and the per-provider bloat adds up before you ever bundle your app. The prisma CLI package has also grown: it now bundles @prisma/studio-core and an embedded Postgres (@electric-sql/pglite) for local development, which explains some of the extra weight but isn't something the size comparison on Prisma's blog post mentions.

What it refuses

Moving the connection string out of the schema file isn't a suggestion, it's enforced:

Error: Prisma schema validation - (get-config wasm)
Error code: P1012
error: The datasource property `url` is no longer supported in schema files.
Move connection URLs for Migrate to `prisma.config.ts` and pass either
`adapter` for a direct database connection or `accelerateUrl` for
Accelerate to the `PrismaClient` constructor.

Construct the client with no adapter at all and you get a real error, not a crash buried three stack frames down:

PrismaClient was instantiated without any options. A driver adapter is
required to connect to your database.

And the old middleware API is gone outright:

> prisma.$use(() => {})
TypeError: prisma.$use is not a function

The documented replacement, a query extension via $extends, does work as a drop-in. I wired up the exact pattern from Prisma's migration guide — intercepting user.create to log the call before running it — and it fired correctly on the first try, which is more than I expected given how much else in this release needed a workaround of its own.

One more packaging detail nobody warned me about: the generated client is TypeScript source, not compiled JavaScript. There's no client.js to require(). I had to run it with node --experimental-strip-types or a bundler step; a project with no TypeScript build step of its own will not run this client as-is.

What I got wrong on the way

My first concurrency test looked like a second strike against the new engine. I fired 50 parallel findUnique calls with Promise.all and the new client took 14-17 ms against the old engine's 3.5-5 ms — three to four times slower, the opposite of the headline number, and I nearly wrote that up as "concurrency regression."

Then I widened the test to 300 parallel calls over three trials instead of one batch of 50. The first trial on the new engine was slow, 56 ms. The second and third were 20.2 ms each — statistically identical to the old engine's 20.2-27 ms range on the same test. What I'd actually measured the first time was a one-off warm-up cost on the very first call of a given query shape through the WASM compiler, not a standing concurrency penalty. A single small batch with no repetition was the wrong instrument for the question I was asking.

What it costs on cold start

This is where the serverless pitch behind this whole rewrite runs into trouble. I split require(), client construction, $connect(), and the first query into separate timings, three runs each.

Stage Prisma 6 Prisma 7.10.1
require/import 51-70 ms 143-157 ms
new PrismaClient() 2-4 ms ~2 ms
$connect() 8.5-9 ms 64-91 ms
first query — 7-11 ms
Total to first query ~69 ms ~236 ms

The new client is about 3.4 times slower from process start to a usable connection, almost a mirror image of the 3.1x it gains back on repeated queries. Removing the Rust binary is specifically pitched as better for serverless and edge runtimes, where cold start is the metric that matters most, and on this measurement it's worse there, not better. A function that serves one request per invocation never gets to the warm, repeated-query phase where the new engine wins.

Run it yourself 

// bench.js — run once against each client, three times each
const dbFile = './prisma/dev.db';
const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
await prisma.$connect();
const t1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
console.log('connect_ms', Number(t1 - t0) / 1e6);

const N = 2000;
const tQ0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
  await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: `u${i}@test.com` } });
}
const tQ1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
console.log('query_ms_for', N, Number(tQ1 - tQ0) / 1e6);

For the Rust engine: npm i prisma@6 @prisma/client@6, a plain datasource db { provider = "sqlite" url = "file:./dev.db" }, then node bench.js.

For the Rust-free engine: npm i prisma@7.10.1 @prisma/client@7.10.1 @prisma/adapter-better-sqlite3@7.10.1 better-sqlite3, drop url from the datasource block, add a prisma.config.ts, generate with provider = "prisma-client", and run with node --experimental-strip-types bench.js after constructing the client as new PrismaClient({ adapter: new PrismaBetterSqlite3({ url: dbFile }) }).

For node_modules size: du -sb node_modules in each project, before you install anything else.

A process that stays up between requests only pays that 236ms once, then keeps the 3x read speed-up for every query after. A function that gets a fresh container on most invocations pays it almost every time and rarely stays warm long enough to earn the 3x back. Which bucket a given deployment falls into isn't something the Prisma changelog can tell you, so it's worth timing $connect() to first query on the actual driver adapter for your actual database, not mine on SQLite, before moving anything that scales to zero onto 7.10.1.

articles.body_html:
Testing Electron Apps: A Practical Guide to Unit, Integration, and E2E Coverage

TL;DR: Electron apps are not just web apps — they are Node main processes, sandboxed renderers, a preload bridge, and an OS-native surface. Testing them with only a Vitest config and a hope will leave your IPC contracts and window lifecycle untested. This post lays out the four-layer testing strategy we actually ship with: unit tests for main-process logic, component tests for the renderer, IPC contract tests that lock the preload boundary, and Playwright E2E that launches the real Electron binary. It also tells you what not to test, so you don't spend three days fighting native dialogs.

Table of Contents

  1. Why Electron testing is different
  2. Layer 1 — Unit tests for main-process logic
  3. Layer 2 — Component tests for the renderer
  4. Layer 3 — IPC contract tests
  5. Layer 4 — E2E with Playwright
  6. What not to test
  7. Pitfalls we hit in production
  8. Checklist

Why Electron testing is different

A browser-only web app has one process and one event loop. An Electron app has at least:

  • a main process running Node.js (window lifecycle, file system, menus, tray);
  • one or more renderer processes running your web UI (sandboxed, no direct Node access);
  • a preload script that bridges the two via contextBridge;
  • and a pile of OS-native bits (dialogs, notifications, global shortcuts, auto-updater).

Each of these layers needs a different testing approach. If you only run renderer unit tests, your IPC handlers are untested. If you only run E2E, every test takes 20 seconds and you will delete the suite the first time it flakes. The goal is a pyramid: lots of fast tests at the bottom, a thin layer of slow E2E at the top.

Layer 1 — Unit tests for main-process logic

Main-process code should be plain TypeScript modules that take dependencies as arguments, not modules that import electron at the top level and call BrowserWindow.getAllWindows() on import. That shape is what makes it testable.

// src/main/project-service.ts
import { promises as fs } from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';

export interface ProjectRepo {
  root: string;
}

export class ProjectService {
  constructor(private readonly fsImpl: typeof fs = fs) {}

  async listRecent(repo: ProjectRepo, limit = 10): Promise<string[]> {
    const entries = await this.fsImpl.readdir(repo.root, { withFileTypes: true });
    return entries
      .filter((e) => e.isDirectory())
      .map((e) => e.name)
      .slice(0, limit);
  }

  async ensureProjectDir(repo: ProjectRepo, name: string): Promise<string> {
    const dir = path.join(repo.root, name);
    await this.fsImpl.mkdir(dir, { recursive: true });
    return dir;
  }
}

The fsImpl injection is the trick. In production you pass the real fs; in tests you pass an in-memory stub.

// test/main/project-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { ProjectService } from '../../src/main/project-service';

function fakeFs(dirs: string[]) {
  return {
    readdir: async () => dirs.map((name) => ({ name, isDirectory: () => true })),
    mkdir: async () => undefined,
  } as any;
}

describe('ProjectService', () => {
  it('lists up to limit directories', async () => {
    const svc = new ProjectService(fakeFs(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']));
    const out = await svc.listRecent({ root: '/repo' }, 2);
    expect(out).toEqual(['a', 'b']);
  });
});

Run this with plain vitest run — no Electron binary, no display. It should finish in milliseconds.

Rule: Anything in src/main that does not touch BrowserWindow, app, or native modules should be importable under plain Node. If importing it requires a running Electron, you have coupled your business logic to the framework and need to refactor.

Layer 2 — Component tests for the renderer

The renderer is just a web app, so you already know how to test it: Vitest + your component testing library of choice. The only Electron-specific twist is that window.electron (your contextBridge exposure) does not exist in the test environment. Stub it globally.

// test/renderer/setup.ts
beforeEach(() => {
  (window as any).electron = {
    projects: {
      list: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue([{ name: 'demo', path: '/p/demo' }]),
      create: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue('/p/demo'),
    },
    shell: { openExternal: vi.fn() },
  };
});

Then your component tests look exactly like web tests:

import { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react';
import { ProjectList } from '../../src/renderer/components/ProjectList';

it('renders projects from the IPC bridge', async () => {
  render(<ProjectList />);
  expect(await screen.findByText('demo')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

it('calls create when the new-project button is clicked', async () => {
  render(<ProjectList />);
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /new project/i }));
  expect(window.electron.projects.create).toHaveBeenCalled();
});

The benefit of stubbing at window.electron rather than mocking your own wrapper is that the preload contract is what you are testing against — if you rename a method in preload and forget to update the renderer, TypeScript will still compile because the stub is any, but Layer 3 below will catch it.

Layer 3 — IPC contract tests

This is the layer most teams skip, and it is the one that catches real bugs. The preload script is a contract between untrusted renderer code and privileged main-process code. Test that contract explicitly.

// test/ipc/contract.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } from 'electron';

// We import the real preload source and run it against a fake contextBridge.
let exposed: Record<string, unknown> = {};
(contextBridge as any).exposeInMainWorld = (key: string, api: unknown) => {
  exposed[key] = api;
};
(ipcRenderer as any).invoke = async (channel: string, ...args: unknown[]) => {
  return { channel, args };
};

// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-var-requires
require('../../src/preload/index.ts');

describe('preload contract', () => {
  it('exposes a typed projects API', () => {
    expect(exposed).toHaveProperty('electron.projects');
    const api = (exposed as any).electron;
    expect(typeof api.projects.list).toBe('function');
    expect(typeof api.projects.create).toBe('function');
    expect(typeof api.shell.openExternal).toBe('function');
  });

  it('does not leak raw ipcRenderer onto the bridge', () => {
    expect((exposed as any).electron).not.toHaveProperty('ipcRenderer');
  });

  it('routes list to the expected channel', async () => {
    const api = (exposed as any).electron;
    const res = await api.projects.list();
    expect(res.channel).toBe('projects:list');
  });
});

The three assertions that matter:

  1. Every method you expect is exposed — renaming or dropping one breaks the build.
  2. Raw ipcRenderer is not on the bridge — a common security slip.
  3. Channel names match what ipcMain.handle registers — pair this with a test on the main side that enumerates registered handlers and asserts they are in the allowlist.

We also keep a single src/shared/ipc-channels.ts that exports channel name constants, and both preload and main import from it. No stringly-typed channels scattered across the codebase.

Layer 4 — E2E with Playwright

Unit and contract tests give you confidence in individual pieces. E2E gives you confidence that the real Electron binary, the real preload, and the real main process work together. Playwright has first-class Electron support, and you should use it.

// e2e/app.spec.ts
import { test, expect, _electron as electron } from '@playwright/test';
import { join } from 'node:path';

test('window opens and shows the project list', async () => {
  const app = await electron.launch({
    args: [join(__dirname, '..', '..', 'out', 'main', 'index.js')],
  });
  const win = await app.firstWindow();
  await win.waitForLoadState('domcontentloaded');

  await expect(win.locator('h1')).toContainText('Projects');
  await expect(win.locator('[data-testid="project-list"] .project')).toHaveCount(1);

  // exercise an IPC round-trip through the real bridge
  await win.getByRole('button', { name: /new project/i }).click();
  await expect(win.locator('.project')).toHaveCount(2);

  await app.close();
});

A few things we learned the hard way:

  • Launch the built output, not electron . against source. Use your compiled out/main/index.js so the E2E is testing what you actually ship.
  • Use app.firstWindow() rather than guessing a URL. Electron windows do not have a useful URL for your main window in packaged builds.
  • waitForLoadState is your friend. Rushing assertions after launch is the #1 cause of flakes.
  • Give each E2E test a clean user-data dir via --user-data-dir=$TMPDIR/... so tests do not share state.
  • Do not click native OS dialogs from Playwright. If your flow opens a dialog.showOpenDialog, stub it from the main process in test mode (see next section).

What not to test

Some things look testable but are not worth the maintenance cost.

Surface Why skip it What to do instead
Native dialog.showOpenDialog / showMessageBox OS-level, platform-specific, unscriptable reliably Inject a dialogService interface; use a stub in tests
Auto-updater network calls Depends on external server, signed updates, real code signatures Unit-test the decision logic (should update? roll back?), never autoUpdater.checkForUpdates()
Tray icon rendering Pure OS compositor Screenshot once manually; do not assert pixels
Global shortcuts Hook into the OS input stack Test the registration/unregistration logic, not the keypress itself
Code signing / notarization External, slow, network-bound Verify on CI with a single dedicated job, not in PR tests
Crash reporter native dumps Requires an actual crash Unit-test the breadcrumb/redaction layer; send one real crash to staging manually

The pattern: test your logic, not the operating system. Wrap the native call behind a tiny interface, test your code that decides what to call, and let the integration points be covered by Layer 4 smoke tests only.

Pitfalls we hit in production

  1. __dirname is not what you expect in ESM builds. Electron has migrated to ESM; if your Playwright launch path is relative, you will silently start the wrong bundle. Use path.join(__dirname, ...) explicitly and log the resolved path in CI.
  2. Preload changes do not hot-reload. When you change src/preload, you must rebuild and restart Electron. Stale preloads are the #1 "works in unit, fails in E2E" bug.
  3. Sandbox enabled means your preload runs in a more restricted context. Node builtins you used in preload will not be available. Keep preload minimal — IPC channel names and argument validation only.
  4. Renderer fetch to local files is blocked by CSP. E2E tests that load file:// resources need the same CSP you ship in production, or you will green-test a broken build.
  5. Playwright and Electron versions must match. A Playwright built for Electron 30 will flake on Electron 33. Pin them together.
  6. app.getPath('userData') is shared across test runs. Two E2E tests writing to the same SQLite file will corrupt each other. Pass a fresh --user-data-dir per test worker.

Checklist

  • [ ] Business logic in src/main imports no electron module at the top level
  • [ ] Main-process services accept their Node dependencies as constructor args
  • [ ] Renderer tests stub window.electron in a global setup file
  • [ ] A contract test enumerates every method on the preload bridge and asserts raw ipcRenderer is not exposed
  • [ ] IPC channel names live in a single shared constants module
  • [ ] E2E launches the built output, not source
  • [ ] Every E2E worker gets a fresh --user-data-dir
  • [ ] Native dialogs and auto-updater are behind interfaces with test doubles
  • [ ] CI runs unit + contract on every PR, E2E on every push to main
  • [ ] Playwright and Electron major versions are pinned together

Testing Electron well is less about choosing a framework and more about drawing the process boundaries clearly. Once your main logic is plain Node, your renderer is a plain web app, and your preload is a tiny testable contract, the actual test files are almost boring — which is exactly what you want.

articles.title: I built a private, offline AI chat you can run with one command: npx unmuzzled
articles.description: A local LLM chat app built on llama.cpp, Node and a hand-built web UI, plus what it took to make localhost secure and ship the same model on Android.
articles.body_html:
Most AI chat apps send every prompt to someone else's servers. I wanted the opposite: a chat app where the model runs on my hardware, works offline, and takes one command to start.

npx unmuzzled

That's Unmuzzled. It's open source (MIT), and this post covers how it works and the problems I didn't expect.

A real run on my laptop. The reasoning streams first, then the answer. Generation is sped up 8×; the real speed (1.7 tok/s) is shown at the end.

What it does

  • Opens a chat UI in your browser. On first run, a setup screen shows the model, its size, your RAM and free disk, and downloads nothing until you click Download (with pause and resume).
  • Runs the model locally through llama.cpp via node-llama-cpp, using Vulkan, CUDA or Metal when available.
  • Streams answers with Markdown and syntax highlighting, and shows the model's reasoning live in a collapsible, timed panel.
  • Supports editing, regenerating and searchable history. Chats are stored only in your browser.
  • Works with any GGUF model: npx unmuzzled --model ./your-model.gguf.

Why it's different

There are great local-AI tools already. Most of them assume you're comfortable with a terminal, model formats and config files. Unmuzzled is built for the person who just wants a private AI that works:

  • Nothing to set up. No Python, Docker or config files. One command on desktop, one tap on Android. The app checks your RAM and disk and fetches the right file; you never need to know what "Q4_K_M GGUF" means.
  • Private by design. The model runs on your device. After the one-time download it works in airplane mode, and there is no account, telemetry or server.
  • No refusal filters. The default model has had its refusal training removed (details below), so it answers questions mainstream assistants decline. That's useful for research, security work and fiction, and it means the judgement is yours.
  • Same experience everywhere. The desktop and Android apps share the same design, the same model and the same reasoning view.

The model

The default is a 9B model with an interesting family tree:

  1. Qwen3.5-9B, the base model
  2. Jackrong/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Qwen3.5-9B, fine-tuned on ~250k reasoning samples generated by DeepSeek-V4-Pro
  3. xtools-at/…-UNCENSORED-heretic, with refusal behaviour removed using Heretic
  4. mradermacher/…-i1-GGUF, quantised to Q4_K_M (5.63 GB)

Every step is Apache-2.0. Despite the name, it is not DeepSeek's model; it's a small Qwen model trained to imitate DeepSeek's reasoning style. Unmuzzled doesn't redistribute the weights; they download straight from Hugging Face.

Because refusal training has been removed, it answers things other assistants decline, and like any LLM it can be confidently wrong. The README has a responsible-use section, and any model with safety training intact works too.

How it works

The whole thing is deliberately small: no framework and no build step on the desktop side.

bin/unmuzzled.js   CLI: arguments, setup state, model download, startup
src/server.js      HTTP server, static files, streaming chat API (SSE)
src/engine.js      node-llama-cpp wrapper, reasoning/answer separation
src/models.js      model catalog, download with pause/resume
public/            the interface: plain HTML, CSS and ES modules

Streaming. The browser POSTs the conversation to /api/chat, and the server streams Server-Sent Events: thought chunks, text chunks, and a final done event with token count and tokens/second. node-llama-cpp separates the model's reasoning into segments; for templates that don't, a small state machine splits <think>…</think> out of the raw stream, including tags that arrive split across chunks.

The UI. I wanted it to look like a carefully made desktop tool rather than a template: warm neutrals, one muted accent, IBM Plex Sans and Mono served locally (so it works offline), hand-drawn icons, and no gradients or glow. Model output is untrusted, so raw HTML is escaped and remote images are never fetched.

The part I didn't expect: localhost security

A local AI server feels private, but any website you visit can try to talk to 127.0.0.1. Two attacks matter:

  • CSRF-style requests. A page can fire a text/plain POST at your local server without a CORS preflight. Unmuzzled requires application/json, which forces a preflight the server never approves.
  • DNS rebinding. A malicious domain can resolve to 127.0.0.1 after the page loads, making the browser treat your local server as same-origin. Unmuzzled rejects any request whose Host header isn't a local name.

The same guard protects the setup endpoints, so no website can start a 5 GB download on your machine.

Honest numbers

On my laptop (Intel i5-1135G7, Iris Xe integrated graphics via Vulkan, 16 GB RAM), the 9B model runs at about 2 tokens/second (1.7–2.7 across my runs) after a ~40–50 second load. "Offline" doesn't mean "fast"; hardware is the whole story. A discrete GPU or an Apple Silicon Mac is many times faster. Reasoning models also generate their thinking before the answer, which adds to wait time on slow hardware.

Shipping it on Android

The Android app (beta) runs the same uncensored model on the phone itself. It's not a thin client for a server or your laptop; once the model is downloaded, the phone needs no network at all.

What using it looks like:

  1. Open the app. It checks your phone's memory and free storage and tells you whether the 9B model will fit (it needs about 12 GB of RAM, which current flagships have).
  2. Tap Download. The 5.6 GB model downloads with a progress bar, speed and time left. You can pause it, and if you leave the app it saves its place and resumes when you come back. The screen stays on until it's done.
  3. Chat. Replies stream in with Markdown and a collapsible reasoning panel. A Think toggle in the composer switches between deep reasoning and instant answers.

Already have a GGUF file? "I already have a .gguf file" imports it from the phone's storage instead. Chats, settings and the model live only on the device, and there's no sign-in.

Under the hood it's React Native (Expo) with llama.rn. It ships llama.cpp builds tuned for modern ARM cores (dotprod/i8mm) and optional OpenCL offload on Adreno GPUs. Download the APK (beta). Open it on the phone and allow installs from that source when asked.

Building it on Windows was its own adventure:

  • Gradle couldn't download anything until I forced Java onto IPv4. The network's IPv6 was broken, and Java tried it first.
  • A Markdown library imported Node's built-in punycode, which doesn't exist in React Native, so I installed the standalone package.
  • Windows' 260-character path limit broke the native build: one library's generated C++ paths reached 297 characters, and Android's bundled Ninja 1.10 can't use long paths. I replaced the library with a 30-line Kotlin module that reads the system bar insets directly.

The app goes on GitHub Releases rather than Google Play. An app built around an uncensored model doesn't fit Play's AI-content policy, and side-loading an open-source APK is a well-trodden path.

Try it 

npx unmuzzled                         # setup screen, then chat
npx unmuzzled --model ./model.gguf    # bring your own model
  • GitHub: https://github.com/rahulagarwal18/unmuzzled
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/unmuzzled

If you run it, I'd love to know your tokens/second and hardware. Issues and PRs are welcome.

articles.title: I built a collaborative pixel art game in a bottle — with 0 npm dependencies
articles.description: 🌊 What is Dear Stranger?   I recently launched Dear Stranger (dearst.app) — a cozy,...
articles.body_html:
🌊 What is Dear Stranger?

I recently launched Dear Stranger (dearst.app) — a cozy, anonymous, collaborative pixel art web game.

The concept is inspired by the old tradition of casting a message in a bottle into the ocean:

  1. Cast a bottle: You start by drawing a few pixel strokes on a small canvas (or choose from 8 classic masterpieces like Van Gogh's Starry Night or Monet).
  2. Drift across the sea: Your bottle travels across the world to strangers.
  3. Collaborate: 2 to 4 strangers take turns painting their fair share.
  4. Returns home: Once complete, the bottle journeys back to everyone who participated, complete with a celebratory replay of each painter's strokes and a travel map showing the countries it sailed through!

Play it directly in your browser (no sign-up required):
👉 https://dearst.app

🛠️ The Tech Stack: Exactly 0 npm dependencies

As web developers in 2026, our node_modules folders often weigh hundreds of megabytes just to render a button. For Dear Stranger, I set a personal challenge:

Can we build a full-featured, persistent, real-time multiplayer collaborative web app with ZERO external npm dependencies?

The answer is yes.

1. Pure Vanilla JS on the Frontend

  • Zero build tools: No Webpack, Vite, or Babel. Browsers have supported native ES modules for years.
  • HTML5 Canvas & SVG: Custom pixel manipulation, touch-enabled zooming/panning, and color palette sampling.
  • Dynamic Voyage Map: Natural Earth 1:50m geographic landmass rasterized into an ultra-compact dot grid rendered with pure SVG paths and beacons.

2. Node.js Built-in Standard Library on the Backend

  • Built on Node's native HTTP server and node:crypto.
  • Pure Web Push: RFC 8291 payload encryption and RFC 8292 VAPID signatures implemented purely with node:crypto — no web-push npm package required.
  • SQLite with WAL mode: Fast, zero-config persistent storage with foreign keys and immediate transactions.

3. Internationalization (i18n) from Day One

The game natively supports 5 languages:

  • 🇰🇷 Korean
  • 🇺🇸 English
  • 🇫🇷 French
  • 🇯🇵 Japanese
  • 🇨🇳 Chinese

Even the system NPC (Lighthouse · Keeper) and world country labels dynamically localize using the native Intl.DisplayNames API!

🎨 Game Design: Solving the "Trolling & Slacking" Problem

Collaborative art on the internet is notorious for two problems: trolls overwriting others' work and slackers drawing 1 pixel and dumping the rest on the next person.

Here is how Dear Stranger solves it through game mechanics:

  1. The 75% Fair Share Quota: Each painter receives an equal allocation of the remaining blank cells. You must fill at least 75% of your quota before the game lets you send the bottle onward.
  2. No Overwriting: Pixels already laid down by earlier strangers are immutable and locked.
  3. Report & Restoration (Kintsugi for pixels): If someone draws something offensive, any player can report that layer. The offender's layer is immediately hidden, and a blank space is created so another stranger can step in to restore the painting!

🖼️ What's next?

We launched with 8 classic museum masterpieces in both guided tracing mode and 64-pixel challenge mode. We plan to continuously add more classical artworks and community features.

Feel free to pick up a bottle, paint a few pixels, and see where your art travels:

🌊 Play the game: https://dearst.app

I’d love to hear your thoughts, feedback, and questions in the comments below!

articles.title: Designing Games for One Shared Phone: 7 UX Patterns From 30+ Pass-and-Play Games
articles.description: Most multiplayer advice assumes every player has their own screen. Pass-and-play games break that...
articles.body_html:
Most multiplayer advice assumes every player has their own screen. Pass-and-play games break that assumption: one phone sits on the table, and it moves from hand to hand. That changes almost every UX decision, from how a turn starts to what "undo" is allowed to mean.

I run Pass and Play Games, a free collection of 30+ browser games built for exactly this: chess, Ludo, dice games, and party games for up to 12 people, all on one device. These are the seven UX patterns that show up across the whole collection.

1. Hide, then pass

The core problem: some information belongs to one player only. Your dice in Liar's Dice. Your role in Mafia. The secret word in Imposter.

The fix is a pass screen between turns. The current player hides their information, hands the phone over, and the next player taps to reveal their own. In our Imposter game the phone first shows a "Pass to Riya" screen that tells everyone else to look away. Then Riya's word sits behind a "Hold to reveal" panel: she holds it to read the word, and the moment she lets go, it hides again. In Liar's Dice, a pass screen covers the dice before every turn.


In Imposter, the word only shows while Riya holds the panel. Let go and it hides.

The rule of thumb: never show private information on the same screen that hands control to the next person.

2. Make every secret turn look the same

A pass screen isn't enough if the turns look different from across the room. In Mafia, if only the mafia spend ten seconds tapping at night, everyone else can guess who they are.

So in our Mafia game, the phone visits every living player at night. The mafia choose a target, the Doctor protects someone, the Detective checks someone, and townspeople answer a harmless question. Everyone taps for a similar amount of time, so watching the person holding the phone tells you nothing.

3. Decide what actually needs to be secret

The opposite mistake is hiding everything. Not every game needs a pass screen, and extra taps slow a party down.

In our Truth or Dare, the phone stays on the table and nothing is hidden: it picks the next player, they choose, and everyone hears the card. In Charades, the secret is hidden from the guesser instead: in Forehead mode, the guesser holds the phone to their forehead while everyone else sees the word.

A useful exercise before building any game: list every piece of information and ask who is allowed to see it, and when.

4. Make turn order impossible to argue about

With one device, "whose turn is it?" causes more arguments than the rules do. Two things help:

  • Names in seating order. Players type their names in the order they're sitting, and turns rotate in that order. The phone always moves around the table in one direction.
  • Fair randomness. In Truth or Dare, "Spin" mode picks the next player randomly, but everyone has a turn before anyone gets a second one. Random enough to be fun, fair enough that nobody gets picked three times in a row.


In Truth or Dare nothing is hidden: the phone stays on the table, shows whose turn it is, and everyone can see the choice.

5. Secret votes that protect people

Group votes on one phone are awkward. If the phone shows who voted for whom, you've built a friendship-ending machine.

Two approaches that work:

  • Show the result, never the voters. In our Most Likely To, a secret vote shows the counts only, never who voted for whom.
  • Reveal only when everyone has voted. In Would You Rather's secret mode, the phone is passed round, each person taps alone, and nobody sees the split until the last vote is in.

Offering both "vote together" (show of hands, fast) and "secret vote" (slower, safer) lets each group pick.

6. Undo that can't be abused

Mis-taps are easy to make when a phone is being passed around, so undo matters. But in a game with dice, a careless undo is a cheat button.

The rule across our games: undo can reverse a decision, but never luck.

  • In Yacht Dice, undo returns your dice, but it never gives you a new roll.
  • In Hot Dice, you can take back a bank, but never a roll.
  • In Liar's Dice, you can undo your own bid, but not after someone has called "Liar!".
  • In Ludo, you can undo moving the wrong token without getting a re-roll.


In Yacht Dice, Undo stays greyed out after a roll. It can take back a scoring choice, but it never gives you a new roll.

7. Never lose the game

A shared phone gets locked, pocketed, or used to check a message mid-game. If that resets the game, the group won't come back.

So saving as you go matters. Liar's Dice saves after every bid, Ludo and Snakes and Ladders auto-save, and in Draw and Guess the drawing itself is saved, so a reload restores the turn. On top of that, every game keeps working offline after the first visit, which matters on road trips, camping weekends and flights.

Bonus: let the computer fill empty seats

"We only have three people" shouldn't stop a four-player game. In most of our board and dice games, any seat can be a computer player, so the game fits whatever group is actually in the room.

What I'd tell anyone building for one shared screen

Design the handover, not just the screen. A lot can go wrong in the two seconds when the phone changes hands: someone sees what they shouldn't, the wrong person taps, or the game loses track of whose turn it is.

If you want to see these patterns in action, the party games collection is a good place to start. And if you've built anything for one shared device, I'd love to hear which handover problem bit you hardest.

I wrote this with help from an AI assistant and checked every game detail against the live game pages.

articles.title: Why Edit-Only Circuit Breakers Miss 39.2% of Agent File Rewrites (Auditing 153 Claude Code & Codex Logs)
articles.description: When I wired a PreToolUse counter on Edit and Write to stop Claude Code from patching the same file...
articles.body_html:
When I wired a PreToolUse counter on Edit and Write to stop Claude Code from patching the same file five times in a row, the agent routed around it through Bash heredocs and Python .write_text() calls.

To see how often that actually happens in real work, I parsed all 153 local Claude Code (~/.claude/projects) and Codex CLI (~/.codex/sessions) JSONL transcripts on my machine (2,581 deduplicated tool calls).

1. Why Edit-only circuit breakers miss 39.2% of file rewrites

Across those 153 sessions, agents performed 199 total source-file mutations:

  • 121 mutations (60.8%) went through structured Edit, MultiEdit, Write, or apply_patch tool calls.
  • 78 mutations (39.2%) went through Bash or codex:exec shell commands (cat <<'EOF' >, sed, tee, .write_text(, open(..., "w")).

In session 01a12a24.jsonl, Codex rewrote brain.py 4 times in a single session purely through shell commands (LPB001 + LPB004). Any hook that only watches Edit and Write never fires on those rewrites. Meanwhile in session 01a1784f.jsonl, fno.py was patched 6 times, including overlapping hunks that reverted lines introduced two turns earlier (LPB003).

2. Three false-positive traps that broke my first parser

My first pass at counting file mutations produced wildly inflated numbers until I inspected the raw JSONL rows:

  1. Read-only python3 and sed inspections (LPB006 filters 570 calls): My initial regex flagged submission.py as mutated 32 times in one session. When I read the transcript, 30 of those commands were read-only python3 one-liners (open('submission.py').read()) and sed print ranges inspecting AST nodes and line numbers. Separating read-only inspections from actual write operators (>, tee, cat <<EOF, .write_text(, open(..., 'w')) removed 570 false positives.
  2. .jsonl vs .js prefix collisions & doc updates (LPB007 filters 218 hits): Without a trailing word boundary \b after file extensions, a regex matching \.(js|py|ts) matches .jsonl as .js, accusing journal.jsonl of being a JavaScript source file 207 times. Normal end-of-task updates to README.md and package.json accounted for another 11 edits that should not trigger code-thrash alerts.
  3. Streaming tool_use.id / call_id duplication (LPB014): Claude Code writes multiple JSONL progress lines sharing the same tool_use.id while streaming a single tool execution. Deduplicating by call ID is mandatory before counting consecutive retries or mutations.

3. Tool-error doom loops & deleted-sandbox CWD escapes (LPB008 to LPB012)

On the execution-loop plane, the 153 transcripts contained 178 failed tool calls grouped into 18 consecutive error streaks:

  • 9-turn consecutive tool-error doom loop (LPB008): In 5f37b3d3.jsonl, the agent invoked Skill("pony tail") (with a space instead of ponytail) 9 times consecutively, receiving <tool_use_error>Unknown skill: pony tail. Did you mean ponytail?</tool_use_error> every single time without changing the argument.
  • Deleted-sandbox CWD escape (LPB010): In 2 sessions, a temporary git worktree was deleted while the agent was still active. The shell printed Working directory ... was deleted; shell cwd recovered to /Users/... and the agent immediately ran rg across the home directory.
  • Identical command retries & empty write_stdin spins (LPB011, LPB012): 20 streaks of >= 3 identical consecutive shell commands (48 wasted calls) and 3 sessions spinning on empty write_stdin polls.

Try loopbrake on your own transcripts

I packaged the auditor and hook generator as loopbrake (zero dependencies, Node.js >= 18):

npx loopbrake
  • GitHub: https://github.com/princejain756/loopbrake
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/loopbrake

What threshold of consecutive edits or tool errors do you use before forcing your coding agent to stop and re-read the module from scratch?

articles.title: Why Third-Party Scripts Are Still the Weakest Link in Modern Web Stacks
articles.description: Every modern web application is built on an uncomfortable foundation of unearned trust.  Engineering...
articles.body_html:
Every modern web application is built on an uncomfortable foundation of unearned trust.

Engineering teams spend months locking down backend infrastructure, setting up strict database firewalls, enforcing encrypted server channels, and putting code through rigorous multi-stage reviews. Then, right before launching to production, a product manager or marketing lead asks to track user analytics, monitor page-load speeds, or embed a customer support chat widget.

Within minutes, a few small script tags are added to the website. Just like that, external code from half a dozen outside companies is invited directly into the browser runtime of every logged-in user. And when one of those external companies gets compromised, no server-side security team on Earth can stop the damage.

The recent exploit on Polymarket — where a hijacked performance-monitoring vendor silently drained over $2.7 million from active user accounts in under an hour—is a stark wake-up call. It proves that client-side supply-chain attacks aren't theoretical. More importantly, it exposes how standard web architecture routinely makes these breaches disastrously easy.

The Anatomy of the Attack: What Actually Happened?

The Polymarket breach wasn't caused by a flaw in the platform's core product, a database leak, or a broken smart contract. The company's internal servers were never actually hacked.

Instead, attackers targeted an external vendor named DebugBear, a third-party tool used to track website speed. By taking control of the vendor's distribution domain through a domain-name compromise, the attackers swapped out the vendor's legitimate monitoring file for a malicious one. Because Polymarket's website was set up to fetch and run that vendor file live on pages where users traded, the injected code executed automatically inside active browser sessions.

The malicious file didn't need to guess passwords or break encryption key pairs. It simply loaded into the same overall browser space as the rest of the application. Once inside, it quietly:

1. Read active user session data straight out of the browser's local memory.

2. Accessed the platform's internal transaction tools already running on the open page.

3. Initiated unauthorized money transfers to attacker wallets using valid, live session tokens.

To the receiving servers and verification networks, every single request looked completely legitimate—because it was generated by an authenticated, active user session.

Why Standard Security Defense Controls Fail

When news of a breach breaks, non-security teams often ask, "Don't we have web firewalls and security filters to catch this?" In the modern client-side environment, traditional defenses fall short for three key reasons:

1. Security Rules Check Origins, Not Behaviors

Most web security policies rely on allowlists. Teams define a rule that says: "Trust any file delivered from this specific vendor web address." When attackers took over the vendor's domain, the web address didn't change—only the content stored on it did. The user's web browser checked its allowlist, verified that the web address was on the approved list, and ran the malicious file without hesitation. Allowing an address only verifies where a file comes from, not what it does once it arrives.

2. Backend Security Systems Are Blind to the Browser

Firewalls and server scanners inspect incoming traffic heading directly to your own servers. Automated testing scanners evaluate code that your own developers write. Neither of those tools can see or analyze an external script fetched directly by an end user's browser from an entirely different company's server.

3. Browsers Suffer from an All-Access Design

By default, web browsers do not separate permissions for different scripts on the same webpage. If your core banking app and a lightweight page-speed tracker run on the same screen, they share the exact same house key. The tracker has full visibility into user input, browser storage, and active buttons on the page. Adding a third-party widget to a financial dashboard is the architectural equivalent of handing your building manager the master key to your personal safe.

Architectural Solutions: Securing the Client Side

If web development is going to move past these recurring supply-chain vulnerabilities, engineering teams must stop viewing third-party code as harmless add-ons and start treating it as untrusted software.

1. Require File Verification Hashes

If an application must load files hosted by external vendors, it should enforce cryptographic hash checking. By storing a digital signature of the vendor file on your own servers, the user's browser can verify that the fetched file matches the expected pattern. If an attacker tampers with the vendor file on their domain, the signatures won't match, and the browser blocks execution.

2. Sandbox Outside Code Off the Main Thread

Analytics and chat widgets almost never need direct access to the main visual surface or internal data store of an app. Running third-party tools inside isolated background workers isolates them completely from sensitive browser memory, stored login details, and payment buttons.

3. Self-Host External Dependencies

Rather than pointing websites to live external URLs that can change at a moment's notice, development teams should download, audit, and host third-party files on their own secure infrastructure. Bringing third-party code under internal deployment pipelines ensures that outside updates cannot go live without automated safety checks and manual approval.

4. Isolate Sensitive Session Storage

Critical authentication tokens and payment actions should never sit in general browser storage where any script on the page can freely read them. Storing key credentials inside locked-down, restricted-access browser containers prevents rogue scripts from harvesting user access even if they manage to breach the page.

The Big Takeaway for Product Teams

Client-side supply-chain attacks succeed because web creators treat external scripts like plug-and-play features rather than full software installations running inside active customer accounts.

The next time a team considers dropping a quick analytics snippet or marketing pixel onto a secure dashboard, the fundamental question shouldn't be "How fast can we set this up?" It needs to be: "If this vendor gets compromised tomorrow, what can their code do to our users?" If the answer is "anything it wants," the software design must change.

Sources & Further Reading:

SecurityWeek: Polymarket Returns $3.9 Million to Traders as DebugBear Cites DNS Hijack

Reflectiz Threat Research: Polymarket Hack: DebugBear Script Drained $2.7M

InfoStealers / Hudson Rock: Polymarket Breach Alert: Wallet-Draining Code Found in a Third-Party Script

articles.title: 100 people bought a mug. The stock went from 100 to 99.
articles.description: I wrote the most normal checkout code there is. Read the stock, check it isn't zero, write stock...
articles.body_html:
I wrote the most normal checkout code there is. Read the stock, check it isn't zero, write stock minus one.

Then I sent 100 buy requests at it at the same time, against a real Postgres database. All 100 went through. The stock went from 100 to 99.

async function buy(id) {
  const { rows } = await db.query("SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1", [id]);
  const stock = rows[0].stock;
  if (stock < 1) throw new Error("sold out");
  await db.query("UPDATE products SET stock = $1 WHERE id = $2", [stock - 1, id]);
}

Nothing in there looks wrong. Here's what happens with just two buyers, Alice and Bob:

What went wrong

Both requests read the stock before either one wrote it.

  • Alice reads 5.
  • While her query is out at the database, Node runs Bob's request. Bob reads 5 too.
  • Alice writes 5 - 1 = 4.
  • Bob writes 5 - 1 = 4.

Two mugs sold, and the stock went down by one. Alice's write didn't fail. It just got overwritten. This is called a lost update.

"But JavaScript is single-threaded." It is, and it doesn't help. Every await is a point where Node goes and runs other code, including another call to the same function. The race isn't between threads. It's between your read and your write.

With 100 buyers, every request read 100, so every request wrote 99. And with 1 mug left and 2 buyers, both orders went through. The last mug got sold twice.

"Just wrap it in a transaction"

That was my first guess too. Same code, inside BEGIN and COMMIT (error handling left out):

await c.query("BEGIN");
const { rows } = await c.query("SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1", [id]);
const stock = rows[0].stock;
if (stock < 1) throw new Error("sold out");
await c.query("UPDATE products SET stock = $1 WHERE id = $2", [stock - 1, id]);
await c.query("COMMIT");

Still wrong. With 100 buyers the stock ended somewhere between 88 and 91, depending on the run.

The transaction did change one thing: Bob's UPDATE had to wait until Alice committed. But Bob was already holding the number 4, worked out from the 5 he read earlier. Waiting doesn't make him read again.

A plain SELECT doesn't lock anything in Postgres. With the default isolation level (READ COMMITTED), two transactions can read the same row at the same time, and that's the whole problem.

(Why around 90 and not 99? The connection pool had 10 connections, so the transactions ran roughly 10 at a time. Each group of 10 read the same number, so each group only counted as one sale. 100 minus about 10 groups is about 90.)

Fix 1: let the database do the math

Don't bring the number into JavaScript at all:

async function buy(id) {
  const { rowCount } = await db.query(
    "UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock >= 1", [id]);
  if (rowCount === 0) throw new Error("sold out");
}

stock = stock - 1 is worked out inside the database, on the current value, while it holds a lock on the row. Bob's update waits for Alice's, then sees 4, not 5.

The AND stock >= 1 does the sold-out check in the same step. If nothing's left, no row matches and rowCount is 0.

100 buyers: stock 0. 1 mug and 2 buyers: one order and one "sold out".

Fix 2: lock the row when you read it

Sometimes the logic doesn't fit in one UPDATE. Then keep the transaction and add FOR UPDATE to the read:

SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE

Now Alice's read locks the row until she commits. Bob's SELECT waits, and when it finally comes back, it returns 4. Also stock 0 after 100 buyers.

The cost is that everyone buying that product waits in line. Fine for a mug. Not great for a row that every request touches.

There's a third way too: add a version column, and only write if the version is still the one you read. If someone got there first, your UPDATE matches 0 rows and you read again and retry. No waiting, just the occasional retry.

The numbers

All four versions against a local Postgres, 100 concurrent buys, starting stock 100, 5 runs each:

Version Orders Stock left
Read, then write 100 99 (every run)
Same, inside BEGIN/COMMIT 100 88 to 91
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE 100 0
One UPDATE 100 0

The thing to remember

If your code reads a value, works something out, and writes it back, ask what happens when another request does the same thing between your read and your write. If the answer is "it gets overwritten", you have a lost update. Threads or no threads.

You can step through all five versions, including the version column one, here: https://software-atlas.haiduc0147.dev/t/race-conditions#lost-update
